fields.text: Which of the following is an example of a mand?
fields.hint: Mand is a term that B.F. Skinner used to describe a verbal operant in which the response is reinforced by a characteristic consequence and is therefore under the functional control of relevant conditions of deprivation or aversive stimulation. One cannot determine, based on form alone, whether a response is a mand; it is necessary to know the kinds of variables controlling a response in order to identify a verbal operant. A mand is sometimes said to "specify its reinforcement" although this is not always the case. Skinner introduced the mand as one of six primary verbal operants in his 1957 work, Verbal Behavior.

fields.text: Who is the founder of Radical Behaviorism?
fields.hint:
B.F. Skinner was the pioneer who founded radical behaviorism, which can be distinguished from the methodological behaviorism that preceded it by it's inclusion of thinking, feeling, and other private events in the analysis of animal behaviors.

Some of the concepts to emerge from Skinner's work include:

  • The cumulative record
  • The S-R-S contingency or Operant Conditioning
  • The "Skinner Box" (or Operant Chamber)

fields.text: Which antecedent increases or decreases the value of a consequence?
fields.hint:
There are at least two general types of antecedents, three if you count prompts:

- SD: short for discriminative stimulus - the SD correlates with the availability of a reinforcer

- MO: short for motivating operation, the MO alters the momentary probability of a behavior and value of a consequence from moment to moment.

Motivating operations can be further sub-divided based on their value-altering effect: Establishing Operations increase the value of a consequence (as a reinforcer/punisher) and Abolishing Operations decrease the value of a consequence (as a reinforcer or punisher).

fields.text:
Billy sees a sign for a gas station and gasoline has typically been available in the past when Billy sees a sign for a gas station.

What type of antecedent is the sight of the gas station sign?
fields.hint:
There are at least two general types of antecedents, three if you count prompts:

- SD: short for discriminative stimulus, and SD signals the availability of a reinforcer

- MO: short for motivating operation, the MO alters the value of a consequence from moment to moment.

There are two types of motivating operations: Establishing Operations and Abolishing Operations. 

EO, or Establishing Operations, increase the value of a consequence, whereas an AO (Abolishing Operation) decreases the vlaue of a consequence over time.

fields.text: Classical conditioning is also commonly referred to as...
fields.hint:
Pavlov's Experiment: Pairing & Respondent Relations

Pavlov's experiment famously (and serrendipitously) documented a process by which a stimulus (S1) can be paired with second stimulus (S2) to cause that second stimulus to impact behavior in the same way as that first stimulus.

For Example...

  • The first stimulus elicits some reflex (i.e., salivating, an increased heart beat, a startle response) and is associated with a biological need - hunger, sleep, sexual behavior, or even a biological "need for activity."
  • The second stimulus is neutral - that is to say, it has no current impact on behavior
  • The first stimulus and second stimulus are repeatedly presented together at the same time (paired)
  • After some period of time, the organism will begin to react to the second stimulus as if it were the first - this is called conditioning!

This is process is now commonly known as Classical Conditioning, Pavlovian conditioning, or Respondent Conditioning. While the names are very different, they do commonly refer to this pairing process.

 

Types of Conditioning

There are many types of conditioning, which can have an impact on how the organism learns. The effect on learning can be to make it more efficient or less efficient. This is done by manipulating the temporal arrangement (order in time) of the Conditioned Stimulus (abbreviated as CS) and the Unconditioned Stimulus (abbreviated as US). Here are some examples (keep in mind this is not an exhaustive list):

  • Forward Conditioning: learning is fastest in forward conditioning. During forward conditioning, the onset of the CS precedes the onset of the US.
  • Simultaneous Conditioning: during simultaneous conditioning, the CS and US are presented and terminated at the same time
  • Backwards Conditioning: backward conditioning occurs when a CS immediately follows a US, and usually has the opposite effect as forward conditioning: that is to say, the organism learns that the CS signals the end of the US. 
  • Extinction: the CS is repeatedly presented but the US does not follow. This, of course, must be done after the CS is already conditioned

fields.text: Which of the following is a type of CONTINUOUS data collection method?
fields.hint:
Continuous Measurement 

Continuous measurement data collection systems capture every possible occurence of a behavior of interest. Some of the benefits of continuous measurement systems is they capture every instance of the behavior, therefore, are much more accurate than discontinuous data collection systems. However, as you can imagine, it can be very burdensome to implement a continuous data collection system (such as a frequency count) for a behavior that is very high-rate or near constant. Similarly, if you are a teacher working in a classroom of twenty or thirty kids, constantly measuring the behavior of just one student while tending to the needs of all the others would be a real challenge!

So while continuous measurement systems are excellent at providing a complete record of the behavior of interest, they are limited by the resources available - it might just not be possible or practical to require data collectors to count each incident of behavior in some way.

Continuous measurement systems come in a variety of different common types, as follows:

  • Frequency - counting each individual event
  • Inter-Response Time - counting the time from the offset (end) of one response, to the onset (start) of the next response.
  • Duration - the number of seconds from the onset (start) of the response to the offset (end) of the response.

 

Discontinuous Measurement 

Discontinuous measurement systems only capture a percentage of the behavior of interest. While they are, as a result of this, inherently less accurate than continuous measurement systems, they are much easier to implement as recording each instance of the behavior is not necessary. Instead, data collectors only need to record a "yes" or "no" value for blocks of time during an interval based off specific criteria, as follows:

  • Whole-Interval Data Recording - recording the behavior ONLY if the behavior occurs for the entire interval (from the beginning until the end of the interval, without stopping!)
  • Partial-Interval Data Recording - recording the behavior if it happens at any point in the entire interval.
  • Momentary Time Sampling- recording the behavior if it happens ONLY at a specific moment at time, between the intervals. For example, if you were observing every 5 minutes, you'd set a timer for 5 minutes and look up upon the timer's alarm and identify (yes or no) if the behavior is occurring in that instant and that instant only.

There are different pro's and con's of each time of discontinuos data recording type. Whole-interval recording is great for behaviors you want to see increase for the entirety of an interval, such as, say, staying in your seat during math class. Partial-interval recording is useful when you want to see a behavior decrease or not exist at all during an interval, such as tantrums during homework time. Finally, Momentary Time Sampling is useful for recording the behavior of large groups of individuals (for whom it would be just too cumbersome to individually record), such as kids playing on a playground appropriately vs inappropriately (whatever your definition of "appropriate" is).

 

A Discontinuos Sampling Measurement Example:

Consider the following example to illistrate how different types of discontinuous measurement systems may report completely different (and possibly misleading!) results from the exact same data set:

Perhaps you are recording data on the following behavior-of-interest, "screaming during circle time." The student engages in screaming at the following points in time:

  • from 9:03 - 9:06, for about 3 minutes and 33 seconds
  • from, 9:10 - 9:15, for 5 minutes and 15 seconds
  • from 9:21 - 9:22, for about 30 seconds

The total duration of screaming (in terms of duration, which is, remember, a continuous measurement) is 9 minutes, 18 seconds out of a period of 25 minutes (about 36% occurence of the total duration for circle time)

We would record a "0" below if the behavior met criteria, and an "X" if it meets criteria. As discontinous measurement records, they would appear as follows:

 

Screaming During Circle Time: Whole-Interval Data Recording:

9:00 - 9:05 9:05 - 9:10 9:10 - 9:15 9:15 - 9:20 9:20 - 9:25
0 0 X 0 0

Thus, for our data set, a whole-interval data recording would report a 20% occurrence rate (1 / 5).

 

Screaming During Circle Time: Partial-Interval Data Recording:

9:00 - 9:05 9:05 - 9:10 9:10 - 9:15 9:15 - 9:20 9:20 - 9:25
X X X 0 X

Thus, for our data set, a whole-interval data recording would report a 80% occurrence rate (4 / 5).

 

Screaming During Circle Time: Momentary-Time Sample Recording:

9:00 - 9:05 9:05 - 9:10 9:10 - 9:15 9:15 - 9:20 9:20 - 9:25
X 0 X X 0

Thus, for our data set, a whole-interval data recording would report a 60% occurrence rate (3 / 5).

 

Our Results:

Remember that the actual duration for this hypothetical behavior was 9 minutes and 18 seconds, or about 36% occurrence of the total duration of our imaginary circle time. 

  • Whole-Interval Data Recording underestimated occurrence at 20% (1 / 5 intervals as "X" or "yes")
  • Partial-Interval Data Recording overestimated occurrence at 80% (4 / 5 intervals as "X" or "yes")
  • Momentary Time Sampling Data Recording over-estimated occurrence at 60% (3 intervals as "X" or "yes")

 

Overall, practitioners are using discontinuous methods more and more, as they are much easier to use and can, with caution and mindfulness, be effective at representing an intervention's impact on a behavior in a useful way. However, as you can see from the example above, incorrect use of discontinous sampling methods could mislead practitioners and misrepresent reality!

 

References:

Fiske, K., & Delmolino, L. (2012). Use of Discontinuous Methods of Data Collection in Behavioral Intervention: Guidelines for Practitioners. Behavior Analysis in Practice, 5(2), 77–81.

fields.hint: Tacts (labeling) is a verbal operant which is controlled by a nonverbal stimulus (such as an object, event, or property of an object) and is maintained by nonspecific (aka, "generalized") social reinforcement.

fields.text:
Tim, a BCBA, always writes his procedures in clear and concise terms so that his staff (and families, too!) can easily understand what is meant by his procedures. He provides complete and full definitions, and avoids using overly specific jargon when the person(s) who will be reading or implementing his procedures are laypersons.

Of the 7 Dimensions of ABA (as originally described by Baer, D., Wolf, M., & Risley, R., 1968), which of the following does the above most closely describe?
fields.hint:
In 1968, Baer, Wolf, & Risley formalized definitions for what "Applied Behavior Analysis" is as a science. This was the first article in the very first journal dedicated to the study of Applied Behavior Analysis, formally.Their original article can be found online, for free, on the government's NCBI website for the journal of applied behavior analysis (If you're asking yourself "should I bother to read that?", the answer is yes, you should!). Their seven "dimensions" (aka, "defining characteristics") of ABA are as follows:

  • Applied: Applied interventions deal with problems of demonstrated social importance.
  • Behavioral: Applied interventions deal with measurable behavior (or reports if they can be validated).
  • Analytic: Applied interventions require an objective demonstration that the procedures caused the effect.
  • Technological: Applied interventions are described well enough that they can be implemented by anyone with training and resources.
  • Conceptual Systems: Applied interventions arise from a specific and identifiable theoretical base rather than being a set of packages or tricks.
  • Effective: Applied interventions produce strong, socially important effects.
  • Generality: Applied interventions are designed from the outset to operate in new environments and continue after the formal treatments have ended.

fields.text: Which of the following is a continuous measurement procedure?
fields.hint:
Continuous measurement procedures include frequency (total event count), duration (total time), rate (frequency per unit time), IRT (time between responses), and latency (time between an antecedent stimuli and the occurrence of a specific response).


Continuous measurement procedures record (or attempt to record...) each response in some fashion. This contrasts to discontinuous measurement procedures, which record the occurrence vs non-occurrence of a behavior at a certain moment in time or across an interval of time. Some examples of discontinue measurement procedures include momentary time sampling, partial interval recording, and whole interval recording.

fields.text:
Preference assessments are formal methods to identify the relative preference an individual exhibits for multiple stimuli when that same person is unable to simply express preferences verbally.

Which of the following is a common method for generating a ranked list/hierarchy for a person's preference for various stimuli?
fields.hint:
Preference Assessments can be used to identify the relative preference a person exhibits for various stimuli. It should be noted that preference does not imply reinforcing value, as the only true way to test if a given stimulus will function as a reinforcer is to directly test it through a contingency with some behavior of interest.

Some types of preference assessments include:

  • Multiple Stimulus without Replacement (MSWO)
  • Multiple Stimulus WITH Replacement (MS)
  • Paired Stimulus
  • Free Operant

 

References:

DeLeon, I. G., & Iwata, B. A. (1996). Evaluation of a multiple-stimulus presentation format for assessing reinforcer preferences. Journal of Applied Behavior Analysis, 29(4), 519–533. http://doi.org/10.1901/jaba.1996.29-519

fields.text: When a stimulus is REMOVED from the environment, and the behavior of interest INCREASES OVER TIME, this is referred to as what type of operant contingency?
fields.hint:
There are three types of consequences, generally speaking, for behavior:

  • Reinforcement: a stimulus that follows a behavior and causes that behavior to increase in probability over time
  • Punishment: a stimulus that follows a behavior and causes that behavior to decrease in probability over time
  • Extinction: a behavior that was previously being reinforced by a given stimulus no longer contacts that stimulus. Extinction is usually followed by an extinction burst - a "spike" along some dimension of a behavior, followed by a dramatic decrease in that behavior similar to the effect of punishment.

Positive and Negative are terms used to refer to how the environment changes. Positive refers to adding a stimulus to the environment, whereas negative refers to removing a stimulus from the environment. There can be both positive and negative punishment and positive and negative reinforcement.

It can be useful to think of "positive and negative" as the first names for a consequential operation, and "reinforcement and punishment" as the last names. When analyzing a scenario, first, think of whether a stimulus is being added or removed - this gives you the "first name" (either positive or negative). Next, identify if a behavior is increasing or decreasing - this will determine the "last name" (punishment or reinforcement).

fields.text: When a stimulus is ADDED to the environment, and this causes a DECREASE IN A BEHAVIOR over time, what type of consequential operation is this?
fields.hint:

fields.text:
Sometimes, behavior analysts will break down a complex chain of behaviors into smaller discrete steps to facilitate teaching.

The learner will then be taught to complete the steps in their logical order, with the completion of the previous step serving as the reinforcer for that step and the discriminative stimulus (SD) for the next step. Finally, the last step in the chain (terminal step) serves as the reinforcer for the whole chain.

What is this called?
fields.hint:
A task analysis is used by behavior analysts to break a complicated task down into a more easily accomplishable sequence of smaller, simpler steps.

Chaining is the process by which one behavior is linked to another, such that the reinforcer for the all steps in the chain (except the last step) is the completion of that step, which also serves as the SD for the next step. The final step's completion usually contacts a conditioned / unconditioned reinforcer that serves as a reinforcer for the whole chain!

An example of a task analysis could be making a sandwich:

  1. Open a bag of bread
  2. Take two slices out
  3. Lay them on a plate, side-by-side
  4. Get the jar of peanut butter
  5. Get a knife
  6. Spread the peanut butter on one side of the bread
  7. Wipe the knife off in the sink, and keep it with you
  8. Put the jar of peanut butter back
  9. Get a jar of jelly
  10. Spread some jelly on the other side of the bread
  11. Wipe the knife off in the sink and put it on the dry rack
  12. Put the two sandwich slices together
  13. Enjoy!

In the task analysis above, you might notice that some of the steps (such as steps 4 - 10) can be completed in a different order and still achieve the same effect. For instance, you could absolutely put the jelly on before the peanut butter. However, it would make little sense to do step 12 befor edoing steps 2 - 10. Sometimes, the logical order of the steps may be insensitive to change (that is, you can mix them up), or it may be sensitive to change (that is to say if you mix them up, the terminal reinforcer will change in quality or be unavailable).

fields.text:
Bill is working as a paraprofessional in a classroom of twenty five children. He is very busy! A BCBA working for the school recently asked him if he could take data on a student's fingernail "hoarding." More specifically, a student in his class will chew his fingernails and then store them in his pencil case or in the compartment of his desk. 

Since Bill is so busy, he offerred to take data on the real or object outcomes of the behavior - in this case, at the end of the day, Bill will clean the student's desk and count any fingernail clippings he finds there (and make a note if he observes any hoarding occurring away from the desk).

In this scenario, what type of data collection is Bill using?
fields.hint:
Permanent Product Measurement refers to collecting data on the real, concrete outcomes of a behavior. Permanent products can come in many forms - such as completed homework assignments, smoked cigarettes discarded in an ash tray, or clumps of hair found on the floor.

For a behavior to be measured using permanent product recordings, the behavior must leave something behind following it's occurrence. This is referred to as a product. This product must last long enough to be recorded by the observer, and be reasonably representative of each occurrence of the behavior. It is up to the analyst to decide, based off the outcome, whether the correlation between product and occurrence of behavior is high enough. For instance, in a scenario involving a cigarette smoker, it is conceivable that the smoker may learn to hide or conceal cigarette butts from observers. Deceptive behavior hinders the reliability of permanent products as a data collection tool. 

Permanent products are advantageous for a few reasons. Chiefly, they do not require an observe to constantly monitor the person engaging in the behavior of interest. Secondly, verification and scoring of the product can be done at a later date by an observer who may require training to score a permanent product effectively (for instance, collecting Zaner-Bloser data on handwriting legibility).

 

Some disadvantages of permanent product recording is that it is possible for an individual to conceal their product, altering their score. It is also conceivable that other individuals in the environment might produce a similar product, confounding their result with the behavior of the person of interest.

fields.text: Reinforcers that acquire their reinforcing properties through pairing with another reinforcer are known as...
fields.hint:
Conditioned reinforcers gain their reinforcing properties through pairing with other conditioned or unconditioned reinforcers.

Unconditioned reinforcers are things that satisfy a biological need, such as food, sleep, water, and other things that satisfy a biological homeostatic need. These are not learned - rather, our bodies are "hard-wired" to react to these stimuli as reinforcers due to their importance to the function of our bodies.

fields.text: Which of the following is true about cumulative records?
fields.hint:
Cumulative Records display a "running total" of behaviors that have occurred over a certain time period. A special thing to note about cumulative records is that they never decrease (slope downward) because they each point on the graph is always one more (+1) than the previous.

 

Bonus fact: B.F. Skinner invented cumulative records!

fields.text:
Kaley, a BCaBA, is working with a young child who is learning to make his own lunch. She is collecting data on how long it takes from when she says "Go make your lunch" for him to initiate opening up his lunchbox and cooking his microwaveable meal. Over the course of several meals, she collects the following data:

Trial #1: 28s

Trial #2: 37s

Trial #3: 48s

Trial #4: 17s

Trial #5: 30s

What type of data collection is Kaley using by measuring the time between an antecedent stimulus and the onset of a target response?
fields.hint:
Continuous measurement procedures include frequency (total event count), duration (total time), rate (frequency per unit time), IRT (time between responses), and latency (time between an antecedent stimuli and the occurence of a specific response).


Continuous measurement procedures record (or attempt to record...) each response in some fashion. This contrasts to discontinuous measurement procedures, which record the occurrence vs non-occurrence of a behavior at a certain moment in time or across an interval of time. Some examples of discontinue measurement procedures include momentary time sampling, partial interval recording, and whole interval recording.

fields.text: Response definitions, sometimes also referred to as operational definitions or behavior definitions, refer to a ...
fields.hint:
An operational definition (aka, response definition or behavior definition) should meet the following criteria:

  1. Objective - the definition, when used by multiple persons, should produce high levels of agreement - that is to say, the score produced by multiple people observing the same behavior would be very similar (if not exactly the same). This is referred to as inter-rater reliability or inter-observer agreement.
  2. Clear - there should be no ambiguity between examples / non-examples of the target behavior
  3. Complete - there should be sufficient detail to encapsulate the target behavior in it's entirety
  4. Concise - the description should be as short as possible without sacrificing any of the above requirements.

fields.text: Which of the following describes differential reinforcement?
fields.hint:
Differential Reinforcement is the provision of reinforcement only the appropriate response (or behavior you wish to increase) and applying extinction to all other responses.

Along the way, a shaping procedure may be used to provide reinforcement for successive approximations of the correct response - that is to say, baby steps towards independent or "more correct" responding (whatever that may mean in the specific case you're dealing with).

Usually, when a learner begins to reliably master a "new step", the next step towards the best form of the response will be selected and only that new best form will obtain the maximal reinforcer and all other responses will be put on extinction (or, sometimes, minimal reinforcement). Extinction is the discontinuing of reinforcement of a previously reinforced behavior.

fields.text:
Todd is walking down main street. To his right, he sees a sign that says "Hot & Fresh Donuts." In the past, that sign has typically correlated with an increased availability of donuts (hot and fresh ones, at that!)

What type of antecedent is the hot & fresh donuts sign?
fields.hint:
There are at least two general types of antecedents, three if you count prompts:

- SD: short for discriminative stimulus - the presence of the SD correlates with the availability of a reinforcer.

- MO: short for motivating operation, the MO alters the value of a consequence from moment to moment.

There are two types of motivating operations: Establishing Operations and Abolishing Operations. 

  • EO, or Establishing Operations, increase the value of a consequence, whereas an AO (Abolishing Operation) decreases the value of a consequence over time.

 

Motivating Operations have both value-altering and behavior-altering effects:

  1. Value-Altering: impacts the value of a consequence, either increasing / decreasing it's effectiveness as a reinforcer or punisher.
  2. Behavior-Altering: increases or decreases the momentary frequency ("likelihood of a behavior occurring")

fields.text:
Bill has not eaten all day, and it's almost dinner time. He sees a donut on the high shelf in the kitchen, and reaches for it while he says "Donut please..." in a zombie-like donut trance. Unable to reach it, he looks up at you emploringly before looking back at the donut, salivating.

 

What type of verbal operant is this, generally speaking?
fields.hint:
Mands are a verbal operant under the control of a motivating operation. In this particular example, the boy sees a donut and reaches for it - suggesting he has a MO for donuts. In addition, he begins to salivate, a reflexive response to the presence of food. This is all pretty compelling evidence that Billy is hungry, and he's manding for donuts.

 

A tact would be a label for a non-verbal stimulus that is maintained by generalized reinforcement - in this context, since the vocalization "donuts" is likely maintained by getting access to donuts (specific reinforcement) it is unlikely to be a tact.

fields.text:
A boy looks up at the sky and sees a bird. He says, "A bird!"


What type of verbal operant the boy's vocalization ("a bird") most likely an example of?
fields.hint: A tact is one of Skinner's elementary verbal operants. Tacts are under the antecedent control of non-verbal stimuli (like pictures, things, etc. - but not written words or text). Tacts are reinforced by generalized reinforcement.

fields.text:
Tommy walks up to Sally and says "Hey, do you know the time?" and Sally responds, "It is 3 o'clock!"

 

Sally's verbal behavior, in this instance, would be best classified as a what type of operant?
fields.hint:
Tommy's behavior is an example of a mand: he is requesting information, or more specifically, what time it is.

Sally's behavior is an example of an intraverbal: she is responding to Tommy's mand by providing the answer.

fields.text:
Cathy says "stop copying me!" and her little brother, Billy, repeats "Stop copying me!"

 

Generally speaking, in terms of Billy's response (repeating Cathy's vocalization), this is most closely an example of which type of verbal operant?
fields.hint: Echoics are, essentially, repeating the vocal speech of another person.

fields.text:
Sam is working with a client who engages in problem behavior during math class. Sam's client, Bob, is now working on math problem accuracy which Sam presumes may help decrease this problematic behavior. Due to time limitations, during therapy sessions, Sam does not have time to grade the math problems immediately - he does this work off-site using Bob's completed math worksheets as physical records of their behavior.

 

In behavior analysis, the term for physical records left behind following a behavior (often used as an indirect measurement of that behavior) is...
fields.hint:
Permanent products are the physical results of a behavior that can be counted to indicate some frequency or total count of behavior. For example, a chef might count the number of salads made by a cook during a dinner rush  to determine that cook's rate of salad production. You could also count the number of cigarette butts in an ash tray to identify the number of cigarettes smoked by an adult, or the number of quiz questions written by Alex (to identify Alex's nightly productivity on his website www.aba.rocks).

 

To be useful as an indirect measurement of behavior, each "product" should correspond to a countable dimension of a behavior of interest. Additionally, they should last a long enough time to be counted by the interested party.

All behaviors produce physical change in the universe, but only some behaviors produce a "product" that corresponds uniquely to the countability of a discrete behavior in a desirable fashion AS WELL AS lasts long enough to be measured.

For example, blowing bubbles produces a a very brief "permanent" product in that bubbles come out of the wand. However, if you tried to count the bubbles a few hours after the bubbles were blown, you're going to be scoring zeroes. Conversely, if you were counting "number of paintings painted" by student artists, you'd be able to check the gallery and, in all likelihood, the paintings would still be there and countable.

Choosing the correct permanent product is important. Many businesses run into the issue of using permanent product measures to promote ethical practice. For example, a healthcare clinic may scramble to backdate and retroactively log supervision and client activity logs when they know an auditor will be visiting the next day. The auditor may be fooled, see the backdated logs and "count" them as proof that they have been following best practice all along. While unethical, this type of behavior can be used to "cheat" systems where contingencies are built around permanent products. If you use a permanent product system, be sure to be on the look out for such "cheating."

fields.text: Which of the following are examples of preference assessments that behavior analysts might use to determine lists of appetitive stimuli?
fields.hint:
A multiple stimulus without replacement (MSWO) is a preference assessment commonly used by analysts to generate hierarchies of preferences for individuals whose preferences may be unclear or difficult to determine.

An array of items is presented (usually 5 - 8) and the student will be asked to choose one. The therapist will record the item picked, allow the student to engage with that item, then remove it for the remainder of the assessment. These steps are repeated until every item has had a chance to be selected or the student has not selected an item on 2 or more consecutive trials.

The resulting list may look like this:

  1. Baseball
  2. Bubbles
  3. Barney Cartoon
  4. Cars 3 Movie (YouTube clips)
  5. Rice Bin
  6. No Selection
  7. No Selection - test discontinued

This type of assessment may be conducted several times, generating data on how often a choice may be picked and in what order. This allows us to generate ranked lists of the average preference of items in relation to other items.

fields.text:
Mrs. Susan has two sons, Tim and Tom, who are both identical twins. The boys rough house and fist-fight a lot, and she does not know what to do with them. Soon, Mrs. Susan makes a new rule: every time the boys rough house or fist-fight, if she catches them, she will take away 15 minutes from their video game play time that day.

After a few days, she notices that the boys stop fist-fighting and rough housing (at least, around her).

 

What type of consequence is the removal of video game time which Mrs. Susan observes decreases the behavior of fist-fighting or rough-housing over time?
fields.hint:
Negative punishment is the removal of a preferred stimulus contingent on a specific behavior which causes that specific behavior to decrease over time.

In this case, we are removing a stimulus - therefore, we know this consequence is negative (by definition - negative just means "Removes a stimulus"). Since the behavior decreases over time, we know the consequence must be punishment, too. This means the consequence must be negative punishment!

fields.text: Skinner described Verbal Behavior according to _________ over _________.
fields.hint: Skinner described verbal behavior in terms of the function of the behavior over the form (aka, topography) of the behavior.

fields.text: An SD can be best described as a...
fields.hint:
An SD is an antecedent stimulus that correlates with the availability of reinforcement. SD stands for "discriminative stimulus."

 

For example, if you were driving along the highway and saw a sign for a gas station, that sign would indicate that reinforcement was available for the behavior of driving to the gas station + purchasing gas (the reinforcement, in that case, would be having a full tank of gas).

 

Another example of an SD could be the hot n' fresh sign outside of a donut shop - when you see the sign lit up, it indicates to you that a particular reinforcer - hot n' fresh donuts - are available should you go inside and attempt to purchase them.

fields.text:
What type of data collection does this describe?

Samantha collected the total number of times Edward slapped the table and said "Well how about that!" during Thanksgiving dinner.
fields.hint:
Frequency is a continuous type of data collection which records the total count of discrete instances of behavior.

You might count any number of things - such as the frequency of utterances of the word "aardvark" in class, or the number of times someone gets an A+ on their math exam.

fields.text:
What type of data collection does this describe?

Sarah collected the duration of time it took her father to finish doing the dishes after dinner, measuring from the onset of washing (putting soap on the first dish) till the offset of washing (drying and putting away the last dish).

Sarah should have helped her father do the dishes, by the way.
fields.hint:
DURATION is a continuous type of data collection which records the total length of time it takes for a behavior to begin and end.

The onset refers to when the duration formally begins.

The offset refers to when the duration formally ends.

fields.text:
What type of data collection does this describe?

Samantha collected the total number of times Edward slapped the table over three separate 1 hour observation periods.

Afterwards, she calculated the total number of times Edward slapped the table per hour.
fields.hint:
Rate is a continuous type of data collection which records the total count of discrete instances of behavior OVER SOME UNIT OF TIME.

 

Rate can be compared when the length of the observation might vary, while Frequency can not be.

fields.text: Which one of the following is an advantage of rate data collection?
fields.hint:
Rate measurements can be directly compared across time periods that aren't the same in length, as they describe a ratio of events per unit time. When the unit of time is the same, the values can be compared.

 

Need an example?

Let's compare rate to frequency and see if that helps!

 

Let's imagine that we have a small child who comes to a clinic for behavioral therapy twice a week. Without telling you anything else, I simply present to you the following data:

  • Monday: 150 episodes of aggression
  • Tuesday: 200 episodes of aggression
  • Wednesday: 200 episodes of aggression

Just looking at that data, we'd say Tuesday & Wednesday weren't very good days. We'd conclude that there was an increasing trend in the behavior (things are getting worse) just on those three data points!

However, let's expand our scenario a little bit. Let's say that our client's schedule is not the same on those three days, and it looks something like this:

  • Monday: 10:00am - 12:00pm
  • Tuesday: 12:00pm - 5:00pm
  • Wednesday: 10:00pm - 6:00pm

 

Now let's compare that data, one more time:

Day Frequency Rate
Monday 150 75 / hour
Tuesday 200 40 / hour
Wednesday 200 25 / hour

 

From this example, we can see that rate can be pretty misleading! Changing the unit of measure changes our analysis of the situation! The behavior appears to be increasing when described as a frequency measure, but is definitely decreasing when described as a rate measure!

 

Moral of the story? Be very careful when selecting a data type - all things considered, it's usually best to use rate when continuously tracking the occurrence of discrete behaviors for the simple reason that it allows you to more effectively compare behavior at different points in time.

fields.text:
The onset to start recording the length of time a behavior takes - specifically, crying (with or without tears) for longer than 10 seconds. The offset is described as the total absence of crying (with or without tears) for at least 10 seconds.

What type of data collection does this most likely describe?
fields.hint:
Duration often has a specific onset and offset -- this refers to when a behavior starts, and when it stops -- basically, instructions when to start and stop the timer! This helps ensure consistency between data collectors.

Therefore, the answer to this question is... duration!

An accelerating trend refers to an overall increase in responding, which will be reflected by an increased value being recorded on the Y axis (dependent variable) on the most recent data points.

fields.text:
DISCONTINUOUS data collection records a sample of behavior, not an exact record of each instance of behavior.

Of the following, which are examples of discontinuous data collection?
fields.hint:
Discontinuous data collection is a type of data collection in which a sample (or "subset") of the behavior is recorded / counted with the idea that the data collected will represent (more or less accurately) the actual amount of behavior happening. It can be more practical to collect data discontinuously, but you run the risk of greater variability or under (or over) estimating your behavior.

The following are common types of DISCONTINUOUS data collection:

1. Momentary Time Sampling - recording data (YES or NO) regarding the occurrence of a behavior at a specific moment in time. This means that if the behavior was occurring for the entirety of the interval, but just happened to briefly stop at the point in time in which we observe the behavior, we might still mark 'no.' This is one of the obvious drawbacks of this data collection scheme. One of the up-sides is that it's relatively resource unintensive - a single data collector could easily take data on many individuals simultaneously without becoming too overloaded.

2. Partial Interval Recording - recording data (YES or NO) if the behavior occurs for any part of a given interval. For example, if the behavior occurs for 1 second or for the entire interval, you would still score it as a single "yes" for that interval. As a result, this type of recording tends to over-estimate behavior, which may be a good thing, depending on what you're trying to measure. For example, if you're teaching someone not to bite their teachers, even 1 second of biting could be pretty painful and disruptive. Therefore, you'd be happy with overestimation as it would help guide treatment decisions in the right direction.

3. Whole Interval Recording - recording data (YES or NO) if the behavior occurs for the ENTIRETY of an observation interval. For example, if the behavior occurs for 59 seconds out of a 60 second observation interval, you would not score that interval! That seems pretty arbitrary, but it has it's benefits - imagine a scenario where you are attempting to take data on many learners who are supposed to be working on independent work. These same learners must raise their hand if they'd like to get up from their table work. You could easily task a single teacher with taking WIR data on 5 or even 10 kids, and if you're interested in seeing an increase in their in-seat, on-task behavior, this would be a conservative measure of those behaviors -- a graph with a score of 100% would truly represent mastery, as even a single second of out-of-seat behavior would cost them an entire interval's score!

fields.text: Select the best definition for differential reinforcement, from the choices below:
fields.hint: Differential reinforcement involves reinforcing members of one response class on a more favorable (for the behaver) schedule of reinforcement while withholding (or providing saliently less favorable) reinforcement to other members of other response class(es).

fields.text: Satiation is a term that refers to what?
fields.hint:
Satiation refers to the abolishing operation on the value of a specific stimulus created by over-exposure to that stimulus.

For example, having eaten a lot of food abolishes the value of food as a reinforcer.

One interesting aspect of "generalized" conditioned reinforcers -- such as money -- is that no "quantity" of money is often enough to cause satiation earning it. Humans frequently exhaust themselves trying to earn money prior to reaching some point where they've "earned enough." This applies to other types of generalized reinforcers as well, such as praise and prestige.

fields.text: Which of the following is something that is true about the BCaBA (assistant analyst) certification?
fields.hint:
Some Things BCaBAs Do:

In many agencies, the BCaBA provides the role of supporting and supervising RBTs. They will monitor the performance of the RBTs and others implementing behavioral services.

They can also assist BCBAs in developing a client's plan, performing assessments, and providing other behavioral services. They cannot independently develop a client's plan.

 

Some Things BCaBAs Can't Do:

A BCaBA cannot supervise BCBAs, and is not able to supervise other BCaBAs - however, they can provide mentorship for other BCaBAs. An example could be a BCaBA requesting mentorship (guidance) when working with a new client population (e.g., they switch from EIBI to geriatric clientele) and they request the guidance of another BCaBA. This mentorship will not count towards their supervision requirement.

As of this writing in Summer 2019, all new BCaBAs must receive supervision from a BCBA for at least 5% of their direct service hours for the first year of their practice, and 2% after that. They also must receive oversight on any programs they develop during that time.

Per the BACB's website (link):

 

The Board Certified Assistant Behavior Analyst® (BCaBA®) is an undergraduate-level certification in behavior analysis. Professionals who are certified at the BCaBA level may not practice independently, but must be supervised by someone certified at the BCBA/BCBA-D level. In addition, BCaBAs can supervise the work of Registered Behavior Technicians, and others who implement behavior-analytic interventions.

fields.text: Which of the following examples below is an example of a VARIABLE RATIO schedule of reinforcement?
fields.hint:
Grandma loves the slots in Vegas! On average, every 30th pull of the slot machine results in a small cash payout. Sometimes the payout occurs on the 15th pull... sometimes on the 45th... but, on average, payout occurs every 30 pulls on the slot machine. Grandma can't wait to hit the jackpot someday!

The above is an example of a variable reinforcement system - the slot machine dispenses reinforcement averaging a payout after about 30 responses. 

 

 

A variable ratio schedule of reinforcement describes an unpredictable ratio of responses prior to the delivery of a reinforcing stimulus.

A classic example is a lottery or gambling - an unpredictable number of responses produces the reinforcing outcome. You could win the lotto on your first play, or on your 10,000th. It is highly random.

Not all schedules of reinforcement need to be so thin (in other words, improbable). In applied behavior analysis, the ratio might be as simple as "an average of 2 responses producing the reinforcer." This type of schedule is preferred when frequent responding is desired.

fields.text: Which of the following is an example of MASS TRIALS?
fields.hint: Mass trials involve the repeated presentation of the same SD (discriminative stimulus) with prompting provided if needed to evoke a specific response. This is frequently done to promote the acquistion of a condition discrimination by repeated exposure to a reinforcing contingency.

fields.text: Which of the following are examples of verbal behavior?
fields.hint:
Verbal behavior is defined as the following:

  1. Interaction between a communicator (doesn't have to be vocal) and an audience.
  2. The audience reinforcers the behavior of the communicator
  3. The function is of prime concern - the topography is secondary.

fields.text: What are the four functions of behavior?
fields.hint:
The four functions of behavior (in layman’s terms - analysts may prefer to use more technical terms, such as social / automatically mediated, positive / negative, reinforcement / punishment) are the following:

  • Escape / Avoidance -- delaying or avoiding entirely a non-preferred stimulus
  • Automatic Reinforcement ("sensory") -- behaviors that produce their own outcome without interaction of another person, such as drinking from a cup, reading a book, or scratching an itch
  • Attention -- receiving interaction or joint activity from another person
  • Tangible -- receiving items from another person

 

It may help to remember S.E.A.T. - sensory, escape, access, and tangible!

fields.text: What does response latency refer to?
fields.hint: Response latency refers to the delay between a specific sitmulus and a response.

fields.text: When we refer to the validity of a measurement system, we are referring to what?
fields.hint:
Data are considered valid when the data are directly related to the phenomena being studied and the reason(s) for recording those data in the first place!

 

For example, was a relevant dimension of the behavior selected for data collection and analysis? For example, if you were working with an individual who frequently elopes into busy intersections, a 99% reduction in elopement might look good on paper, but there's still a chance of the individual being struck by a car. However, if you are working on improving an individuals ability to stay on task during math class, a 99% increase would be substantial. This difference is usually described as the social validity of a measure.

fields.text: What does onset refer to?
fields.hint:
Onset and Offset are two terms used to refer to when to start and stop data collection for a given behavior.

 

For example:

 An "episode" of aggression might include a variety of aggressive acts, such as biting, kicking, and pinching. To make data collection easier - and allow a therapist to focus on protecting themselves and their client from harm as opposed to taking data! - we might first objectively define aggression and then use episodes of aggression defined as "onset beginning with the first aggressive act, and an offset following a period of calm of at least 5 seconds without any aggressive behavior."

Of course, this won't give us as precise a measure as we might like, but it can be useful. Some additional considerations might include a concern that episode count might decrease, but the length of episodes might increase or remain higher than desired, which may threaten the social validity of this measure.

fields.text: What does reliability of a measurement system refer to?
fields.hint:
Reliability refers to the extent at which a measure produces the same value upon repeated testing. For example, if you use a thermometer to measure a child's temperature, a reliable thermometer would produce the same measurement (temperature) every time you used it.

Now, that doesn't necessarily mean the measure is correct - the thermometer could, for example, reliably say "101 degrees Fahrenheit" when the reality is the child has a normal temperature. That may be great for a kid looking for an excuse to skip math class, but not so great for a school nurse who's thermometer is not able to identify the true value for the child's temperature.

Based on the data displayed on the graph below, what is the likely function of the client's problem behavior?

 

Having trouble viewing the graph? Click here: https://imgur.com/eTn2xEg.png

Note: be careful of iatrogenic effects when conducting functional assessments with tangibles. Iatrogenic means "caused by the [medical] assessment" and it's important to consider that providing a positive reinforcer contingent upon problem behavior may simply create a new function for that problem behavior! So, tread lightly when using tangible as test conditions!

fields.text: Which of the following is the name for the type of preference assessment where the individual is offerred an array of likely preferred items (typically 5 - 7). As each item is selected, it is removed from subsequent presentations of the array until the learner has selected each item from the array.
fields.hint:
A multiple stimulus without replacement (MSWO - yes, I know, the acronym MSWO is missing the "r" so that's confusing!) preference assessment involves the presentation of typically 5 - 7 items at a time to determine which items are the most preferred and create a hierarchy of those items. Since the items are not "replaced", when the item is selected, it's gone for the remainder of that assessment, so typically the highest value items are selected first. This assessment is often repeated several times to determine the average "rank" of each item in the array.

It's best practice for behavior analysts to rotate the position of each item in the array to ensure that the individual is not just "choosing the item on the right side" (or exhibiting some other kind of position bias).

Food items are typically not intermixed with tangible items during preference assessments, as research suggests that some individuals may exhibit preference for food items over tangible items and skew results of such intermixed assessments.

fields.text: Which of the following is a preference assessment where the individual is systematically exposed to many stimuli in sets of two - this arrangement allows for each item to be presented an equal number of times, which enables us to create a "preference hierarchy" (i.e., how much each item is preferred / non-preferred).
fields.hint:
A paired choice preference assessment involves the presentation of 2 items at a time from a larger list (usually 7 - 12 items) to determine which items are the most preferred. Each item is presented in combination with every item on the list, so that the individual is given an opportunity to "choose" which item they like the most in a contest against every other item.

Often times, behavior analysts will ensure that the position (on the left, or on the right) of the various stimuli is evenly rotated to ensure that the individual is not just "choosing the item on the right side" (or exhibiting some other kind of position bias).

Food items are typically not intermixed with tangible items during preference assessments, as research suggests that some individuals may exhibit preference for food items over tangible items and skew results of such intermixed assessments.

fields.text:
Which of the following is the name for the type of preference assessment described below?

This stimulus preference assessment has a participant select one item at a time from an array of potentially preferred stimuli. Each time they select an item from the array, they can select that item again on the next trial. This continues while the analyst records the number of times each item is chosen, generating a list of most highly preferred stimuli.
fields.hint:
A multiple stimulus with replacement preference assessment involves the presentation of typically 5 - 7 items at a time to determine which items are the most preferred and allow you to identify what is the "most valuable" item(s) from the array. Typically, one item will stand out from it's peers in the array - such as a special toy, like a blankie, or the iPad, etc. - that the individual will choose each and every time they are given the option to. Knowing what this stimulus is on a day-to-day basis can make these types of preference assessments incredibly valuable, especially for learners who have difficulty communicating their choice.

It's best practice for behavior analysts to rotate the position of each item in the array to ensure that the individual is not just "choosing the item on the right side" (or exhibiting some other kind of position bias).

Food items are typically not intermixed with tangible items during preference assessments, as research suggests that some individuals may exhibit preference for food items over tangible items and skew results of such intermixed assessments.

fields.text: Which of the following is the name for the type of preference assessment where the individual is allowed to freely roam a room seeded with potentially preferred stimuli while the analyst records the duration of engagement with each item in the room, hoping to gather an understanding of what items, if any, the individual spends their time with when allowed to freely interact with them, and potentially create a hierarchy out of the amount of time they allocate their responding?
fields.hint:
A free operant preference assessment allows learners freedom to roam an area, such as a play room, and interact with any items in the room they find motivating. The duration of engagement is recorded for each item, allowing analysts to compare the amount of time the individual spent with each item, and therefore determine if one item was more "valuable" than another simply by comparing the quantity of time the individual allocated to interacting with one item(s) over other(s).

Typically, these rooms are "seeded" with likely high-preference items based off care-giver / parent / guardian report, which increases the likelihood of the assessment being successful at generating a hierarchy (or ranking) of preferred items.

Food items are typically not intermixed with tangible items during preference assessments, as research suggests that some individuals may exhibit preference for food items over tangible items and skew results of such intermixed assessments.

fields.text: A _____________ (fill in the blank) is a type of assessment that allows analysts to determine the "why" (or reinforcers) for a specific behavior by arranging test conditions which manipulate antecedents & consequences in an alternating design to evoke (and reinforce) problem behavior. After the assessment, the test conditions are compared with the goal of discriminating what test condition evoked the most problem behavior (and is, therefore, likely a functional reinforcer for that problem behavior).
fields.hint:
A functional analysis is a type of functional assessment where consequences are manipulated in an alternating design to demonstrate which consequences are likely functional reinforcers for a given behavior.

It can be odd to conduct a functional analysis as the goal is unusual - from the onset, you are attempting to reinforce problem behavior. By testing multiple types of potential reinforcers, you identify what type of antecedents and consequences likely evoke and reinforce that problem behavior.

fields.text: A __________ (fill in the blank) is a type of assessment where stimuli are presented to an individual in a systematic fashion with the overall goal of determining what, if any, of the stimuli are preferred by that individual - these “preferred” stimuli may be then used as reinforcers.
fields.hint:
A preference assessment allows us to determine what stimuli are (and are not) preferred by an individual, by measure of how much time they spend interacting with an item (or the frequency of times they choose that item from an array of other items).

PLEASE NOTE: preference does not necessarily imply reinforcing value - for example, if you offerred me a plate with $1.00, a skittle, an M&M, and a smiley face sticker on it, each time I would choose the $1.00. You might write down "$1.00 is the most preferred item" and then attempt to use it as a reinforcer for a variety of tasks. If one of the tasks was touching my nose, sure, I'd be likely to find that $1.00 very reinforcing for that behavior. However, if you change the response requirement to "mowing your massive front yard" I am unlikely to find that $1.00 very reinforcing - my motivating operations will be changed by the response requirement, in this case! So keep that in mind when utilizing the results of your preferrence assessments (or look up reinforcer assessments in JABA).

fields.text:
A therapist is working with a client with limited vocal language. This child is stacking blocks on a table. As he interacts with the blocks, the therapist periodically asks the client what color, shape, and comparative size the blocks are as the child plays.

 

What type of teaching strategy is this?
fields.hint: Incidental teaching involves following the clients motivating operations and using those naturally occurring MOs to contrive opportunities to use language, functional skills, or engage in other behaviors of interest.

fields.text: Which of the following is typically NOT included as an essential component in a skill acquisition plan?
fields.hint:
The following are example of essential components of a skill acquisition program:

  • Materials - what items, if any, are needed to complete the program.
  • Long Term Goal (or, Long Term Objective) - typically achieved in a six to twelve month time frame, with a broad and general statement such as “student will read sight words at the 2nd grade level” or “student will be able to prepare, consume, and put away snack materials without going off task.” A long term goal (LTG) will generate several suitable short term goals, which allow you to focus treatment decisions and begin to identify discrete behaviors for that skill that might need to be taught.
  • Short Term Goal (or, Short Term Objective) - typically achieved on the time frame of a few weeks to a few months, short term goals are collections of specific related skills that support the long term goal. Continuing the example above with a long term goal of “student will read sight words at the 2nd grade level,” some examples of supporting short term goals could include identifying letters printed in a variety of fonts, mastering 50 sight words, and decoding unknown words using phonics.
  • Learn Unit - “The learn unit consists of the inter-locking operants of instruction that incorporate particular student and teacher interactions that predict whether student behavior will be controlled by particular stimuli and setting events.” (Greer, 1994a). This is a description, essentially, of how to teach (and respond to) the behavior of a learner. You will typically encounter this in the form of a written “ABC” (antecedent, behavior, consequences) for the skill being taught.
    • Response Definition - Objective description of the target behavior
    • Antecedent - the MOs, SDs, and any other setup that needs to be arranged prior to the behavior occurring
    • Consequence - typically, the teacher/interventionists response, usually providing a specifically prescribed reinforcer or punisher differential to the “correctness” of the learner’s response.

 

Sources:

Long term goals and objectives:

  • Schloss, P. J. & Smith; J. A. (1998). Applied Behavioral Analysis in the Classroom (2nd ed.). Boston: Allyn & Bacon.

 

The Learn Unit

  • Greer, R. D., & McDonough, S. H. (1999). Is the learn unit a fundamental measure of pedagogy? The Behavior Analyst, 22(1), 5–16.

fields.text: Which of the following is typically NOT included as an essential component in a skill acquisition plan?
fields.hint:
The following are example of essential components of a skill acquisition program:

  • Materials - what items, if any, are needed to complete the program.
  • Long Term Goal (or, Long Term Objective) - typically achieved in a six to twelve month time frame, with a broad and general statement such as “student will read sight words at the 2nd grade level” or “student will be able to prepare, consume, and put away snack materials without going off task.” A long term goal (LTG) will generate several suitable short term goals, which allow you to focus treatment decisions and begin to identify discrete behaviors for that skill that might need to be taught.
  • Short Term Goal (or, Short Term Objective) - typically achieved on the time frame of a few weeks to a few months, short term goals are collections of specific related skills that support the long term goal. Continuing the example above with a long term goal of “student will read sight words at the 2nd grade level,” some examples of supporting short term goals could include identifying letters printed in a variety of fonts, mastering 50 sight words, and decoding unknown words using phonics.
  • Learn Unit - “The learn unit consists of the inter-locking operants of instruction that incorporate particular student and teacher interactions that predict whether student behavior will be controlled by particular stimuli and setting events.” (Greer, 1994a). This is a description, essentially, of how to teach (and respond to) the behavior of a learner. You will typically encounter this in the form of a written “ABC” (antecedent, behavior, consequences) for the skill being taught.
    • Response Definition - Objective description of the target behavior
    • Antecedent - the MOs, SDs, and any other setup that needs to be arranged prior to the behavior occurring
    • Consequence - typically, the teacher/interventionists response, usually providing a specifically prescribed reinforcer or punisher differential to the “correctness” of the learner’s response.

The Learn Unit

fields.text: Stimulus transfer is the process of transferring stimulus ______ from one set of antecedent variables to another, typically using prompting and prompt fading.
fields.hint:
“Stimulus control refers to a change in operant behavior that occurs when a particular type of stimulus (SD or SΔ) is presented. With an SD, the behavior occurs in the presence of that stimulus and does not occur in its absence. With an SΔ, the behavior does not occur in the presence of that stimulus. Stimulus control develops when a given response is repeatedly reinforced in the presence of a particular stimulus (SD) and not in its absence, or not in the presence of a different stimulus (SΔ). Transfer of stimulus control occurs when behavior initially evoked (controlled) by one SD comes under the control of a different SD.”

Bloh, C. (2008). Assessing Transfer of Stimulus Control Procedures Across Learners With Autism. The Analysis of Verbal Behavior, 24(1), 87–101.

fields.text:
A behavior tech is showing a car to a student. They were asked to use a stimulus transfer procedure to teach the client to mand for the car.

When the student is shown the car, the tech waits for 5 seconds before providing the echoic prompt “car”, pausing for 2 - 3 seconds to allow the student to repeat the echoic prompt. If the student says “car,” they are given the car; otherwise, after 3 repetitions of the echoic prompt (and brief delay), the client is just given the item. After several days of intense training, the client begins to produce the vocal mand “car” more reliably, the behavior tech fades out the use of the echoic prompts altogether as the client begins to produce the mand independently and consistently.

 

What type of stimulus transfer procedure is this?
fields.hint: The therapist is using an echoic model prompt in an attempt to teach a mand. The behavior is initially under the control of the MO for the item (in sight) plus the echoic prompt. As teaching progresses, the echoic prompt is faded out entirely and the learner is able to independently mand “car.” Therefore, this is an echoic-to-mand transfer procedure.

fields.text: A therapist is working with a client on tooth-brushing in a task-analyzed format. The therapist is teaching the entire set of steps in the task analysis, which means they are employing what method of task analysis training?
fields.hint: Total or Whole Task training refers to the teaching all of the steps in a task analysis and providing reinforcement differential to independence on the entire set of skills.

fields.text: Position bias refers to what?
fields.hint: Position bias refers to responding that is under the control (undesirably) of the position of the item in an array. For example, if a learner is asked “hand me the green” card, and they typically always select the card to their right regardless of it’s color, that would be an example of position biased responding.

fields.text: When planning a client’s training to generalize a skill to other people, places, or settings, what should an analyst NOT do?
fields.hint:
Train and hope was described by T.F Stokes and Donald Baer as:

“After a behavior change is effected through manipulation of some response consequences, any existent generalization across responses, settings, experimenters, and time, is concurrently and/or subsequently documented or noted, but not actively pursued.”

 

What does this mean?

Some analysts fall into the trap of simply “hoping” that generalization will occur without actively programming for it - as described in their original article, there are at least 7 suggested methods by which an analyst can actively promote generalization of a skill across time, people, and places.

  1. Sequential Modification - when transferring stimulus control from one setting to another, allow for small successive approximations from the initial comntrolling stimulus to progressively different variations of the stimulus until, eventually, the dimensions of the SD have been altered sufficiently and the terminal stimulus has effective control of the target behavior. 
  2. Introduce to Natural Maintaining Contingencies - plan to fade any artificially dense schedule of reinforcement towards the active schedule in the client’s natural environment.
  3. Train Sufficient Exemplars - introduce the learner to sufficient variants of the target stimuli such that reinforcement has been contacted for engaging in the response when a wide variety of non-critical elements of the SD / relevant dimensions for stimulus transfer have been varied or removed - i.e., tacting “bird” when shown a variety of birds of different colors, shapes, sizes (all non-critical elements of the class of animal) whereas some features will likely be consistent across all exemplars (has wings, a beak, feathers, etc.)
  4. Train Loosely - little or no effort is made to control (in an experimental / highly consistent manner) the presentation of the stimuli and the range of acceptable answers is broadened.
  5. Use Indiscriminable Contingencies - during teaching, use or fade towards intermittent schedules of reinforcement to mirror the likely schedule(s) that will be encountered naturalistically. Additionally, if necessary, make it hard to determine when the behavior will contact reinforcement and when it will not, to promote responding even in contexts where reinforcement is not likely to occur.
  6. Program Common Stimuli - plan to use stimuli that are relevant to the learner and will likely be encountered in the day-to-day natural environment. For example, if you are teaching the child tacts, teach them first things they see on their daily routine - their lunchbox, a doorknob, a car, etc.
  7. Mediating Generalization - establishing a sufficiently broad response when learning a new skill that it is likely to be employed in other types of skills - i.e., a child who is being taught how to cut on a dashed line to make animal cut-outs allows a learner to cut out different shapes of animals, which may include untrained exemplars.
  8. Train to Generalize - consider generalization itself an operant that can be reinforced. When the learner engages in novel generalized behavior, provide reinforcement for that behavior (or differential reinforcement for approximations of generalized responding).

fields.text: Food, sex, water, breathable air and any other stimuli that are necessary for life (homeostasis) are what types of _________ reinforcement?
fields.hint:
Unconditioned Reinforcers are types of reinforcers that have phylogenetically reinforcing value - that is to say, their reinforcing value is derived from their direct influence on an organisms genetics - typically, this will be things like food, breathable air, sex, water, and some things that may be specific to the species examined, such as “burrowing spaces” for animals such as guinea pigs that may reflexivly seek shelter when loud startling noises are heard.

 

Conditioned Reinforcers - stimuli that are paired repeatedly with unconditioned reinforcers (food, water, shelter, etc.) may acquire reinforcing value themselves. Additionally, previously conditioned reinforcers (such as movie tickets, which can be exchanged for access to a movie theater) can be paired with a previously neutral (or even aversive) stimulus to alter it’s value. For example, getting free movie tickets in exchange for donating blood was a strategy employed by the makers of the Saw horror movie franchise, and it was reinforcing enough to increase blood drive participation markedly.

For example, money is typically used to purchase a wide variety of reinforcers by humans - infants, however, will find little reinforcing value from currency aside from, perhaps, oral or visual stimulation. As time goes on, they will experience reinforcement through the stimuli money Is exchanged for, such as movie tickets, bubble gum, cigarettes, and cars. Behaviors that produce money on various schedules of reinforcement - such as allowances, chore money, their first paying jobs, etc. - will subsequently condition those behaviors that earn money as reinforcing as well.

 

Ontogenic properties are properties of a stimulus that are learned. The phylogenetic properties of stimuli serve as the basis from which ontogenetic learning will evolve. A common criticism of behavior analysis is that behavior analysts ignore the impact of genetics - this is not true! Behavior analysts should know and understand the evolutionary, genetic root of respondent behaviors, and how those roots grow into the many operant behaviors exhibited by all organisms.

fields.text: A therapist provides a “star” token every 5 times (exactly)\\ the learner responds correctly. After 5 tokens, the learner can exchange the tokens for a reinforcer from the reinforcer menu. What type of schedule of reinforcement is this?
fields.hint:
Fixed Schedules of Reinforcement

Fixed Ratio schedules of reinforcement involve the delivery of a reinforcer at a fixed interval - such as every 5 independent responses.

 

Fixed Interval schedules of reinforcement involve the delivery of a reinforcer following an interval of time, such as every 5 minutes the first response will contact reinforcement.

 

Intermittent Schedules of Reinforcement

Variable Ratio schedules of reinforcement involve the delivery of reinforcers intermittently - that is, “on average” every so often, responses are reinforced. You may observe a variable ratio schedule in action while in a classroom: students may raise their hands to answer a teacher’s question, but the teacher may only call on one student out of the 5 or 6 that may attempt to answer the question. The teacher may attempt to evenly give each kid a turn, resulting in, on average, a 1 in 6 chance of being called on - this would be an example of a variable (a.k.a., intermittent) schedule of reinforcement. 

Gambling behavior is on a variable schedule of reinforcement, and is an active area of research for scientists studying non-chemical addictions such as disorderly gambling or overplaying video games with chance-based objectives, such as World of Warcraft or anything made by EA (electronic arts).

Variable Interval schedules of reinforcement involve the delivery of a reinforcer following a variable delay from the last delivery of the reinforcer. For example, a dog may approach a human with his leash in his mouth several times throughout the day, with the likelihood of reinforcement (in the form of being taken on a walk) being lower if the dog has just got back from a walk, but much higher if the dog has not been on a walk in many hours. On average, mands for going for a walk in this fashion may be reinforced every 2 - 3 hours — this would be an example of a variable interval schedule.

fields.text:
A therapist provides a “star” token on average every 5 times the learner responds correctly - for example, the learner earned a star token after 7 correct responses, 4 correct responses, 6 correct responses, and 3 correct responses, averaging out to an average of 5 responses/token.

What type of schedule of reinforcement is this?
fields.hint:
Fixed Schedules of Reinforcement

Fixed Interval schedules of reinforcement involve the delivery of a reinforcer following an interval of time, such as every 5 minutes the first response will contact reinforcement.

fields.text:
A dog approaches a human with it’s leash in his mouth throughout the day. The human will only walk the dog if it's been a few hours since the last walk, but that amount of time varies depending on the weather, if the human feels like going for a walk, etc. The amount of time varies, but is generally around 2 hours on average, but is sometimes as short as 30 minutes and sometimes as long as 5 hours!

 

What type of schedule of reinforcement does this most closely resemble?
fields.hint:
This is an example of a variable interval schedule of reinforcement because the first response (bringing the leash to the human) made by the dog after a varying interval of time is reinforced by the human's behavior of taking the dog for a walk.

fields.text:
A group of students is usually very motivated to answer their teacher's questions throughout the class. The teacher, trying to be fair, will call on each student as equally as possible. On average, this means that each of the 5 children who typically raises their hands gets called on once every 5 to 7 questions (on average) when the teacher asks a question to the class.

 

What type of schedule of reinforcement does this example most closely resemble?
fields.hint:
Fixed Schedules of Reinforcement

Fixed Ratio schedules of reinforcement involve the delivery of a reinforcer at a fixed interval - such as every 5 independent responses.

 

Fixed Interval schedules of reinforcement involve the delivery of a reinforcer following an interval of time, such as every 5 minutes the first response will contact reinforcement.
