fields.text:
The ABLLS-R (Assessment of Basic Language & Learning Skills) is a popular assessment for individuals with special needs, especially ASD. The ABLLS-R is arranged with skills organized into related groups, such as motor, labeling, social skills, etc. creating an easy to follow curriculum for that child. Each skill is broken down into instructional targets with objective criteria for mastery, with specific response criteria for each objective.

This is an example of what type(s) of assessment?
fields.hint:
What follows are descriptions for various types of assessments - some assessments might meet all, some, or none of the criteria below. It is important to be familiar with these terms before using an assessment, so that you understand the implications of the assessment you are working with.

 

Developmental assessments are linked to the individual’s chronological age (how old they actually are) versus how old they are in terms of the skills they have learned in contrast to the skills typically learned by that age. This is referred to as their “developmental age.” The goal for clinicians using a developmental assessment is to calculate the difference between the client’s chronological age and their developmental age, attempting to “close the gap” as quickly and efficiently as possible.

 

Criterion-based assessments involve presenting skills with specific criteria (an objective performance measure) that need to be mastered before the skill is considered mastered. These skills are typically organized into long-term goals, short-term goals, and instructional goals (from broader to narrow focus) for the convenience of the professional using the assessment. 

 

Curriculum-based assessments are assessments organized in a progressive manner, with suggestions and guides for progressing from one skill to the next as part of a coordinated curriculum. They give you examples of what to teach and in what order, and may also include teaching materials (such as worksheets, manipulative, sight word decks, etc.).

 

Social skills assessments directly target social behaviors and often require the presence of one or more (or even groups) of similarly skilled peers. This is one of the inherent limitations of a social skills program - if the client does not have access to an environment with similar peers from whom social behaviors can contact reinforcement, no social skills program will be effective. Social skills curricula typical emphasize skills such as verbal behavior, understanding body language, defining and interpreting emotions of yourself and others, and other similar behaviors that typically produce socially mediated reinforcers. This can also include some “a-social” skills, such as brushing your teeth or wearing deodorant, as these skills impact your relationships with others (being “stinky” might repel others). 

 

Norm-referenced assessments calculate a quotient score, which can be compared against a standard of deviation to determine where the user performs compared to other persons using the assessment. For example, a score of 100 is “average” and reflective of typical performance on that assessment by typical members of the population the assessment is designed for (i.e., school kids in the first grade, or children at the age of 5). A score of 120 would be above average, and a score of 80 would be below average.

fields.text: A free operant preference assessment is...
fields.hint:
A preference assessment allows us to determine what stimuli are (and are not) preferred by an individual, by measure of how much time they spend interacting with an item (or the frequency of times they choose that item from an array of other items).

PLEASE NOTE: preference does not necessarily imply reinforcing value - for example, if you offerred me a plate with $1.00, a skittle, an M&M, and a smiley face sticker on it, each time I would choose the $1.00. You might write down "$1.00 is the most preferred item" and then attempt to use it as a reinforcer for a variety of tasks. If one of the tasks was touching my nose, sure, I'd be likely to find that $1.00 very reinforcing for that behavior. However, if you change the response requirement to "mowing your massive front yard" I am unlikely to find that $1.00 very reinforcing - my motivating operations will be changed by the response requirement, in this case! So keep that in mind when utilizing the results of your preferrence assessments (or look up reinforcer assessments in JABA).

 

There are many types of preference assssments - here are the different types:

 

Multiple Stimulus WITH Replacement

A multiple stimulus with replacement preference assessment involves the presentation of typically 5 - 7 items at a time to determine which items are the most preferred and allow you to identify what is the "most valuable" item(s) from the array. Typically, one item will stand out from it's peers in the array - such as a special toy, like a blankie, or the iPad, etc. - that the individual will choose each and every time they are given the option to. Knowing what this stimulus is on a day-to-day basis can make these types of preference assessments incredibly valuable, especially for learners who have difficulty communicating their choice.

It's best practice for behavior analysts to rotate the position of each item in the array to ensure that the individual is not just "choosing the item on the right side" (or exhibiting some other kind of position bias).

Food items are typically not intermixed with tangible items during preference assessments, as research suggests that some individuals may exhibit preference for food items over tangible items and skew results of such intermixed assessments.

 

Multiple Stimulus WITHOUT Replacement (MSWO):

A multiple stimulus without replacement (MSWO - yes, I know, the acronym MSWO is missing the "r" so that's confusing!) preference assessment involves the presentation of typically 5 - 7 items at a time to determine which items are the most preferred and create a hierarchy of those items. Since the items are not "replaced", when the item is selected, it's gone for the remainder of that assessment, so typically the highest value items are selected first. This assessment is often repeated several times to determine the average "rank" of each item in the array.

It's best practice for behavior analysts to rotate the position of each item in the array to ensure that the individual is not just "choosing the item on the right side" (or exhibiting some other kind of position bias).

Food items are typically not intermixed with tangible items during preference assessments, as research suggests that some individuals may exhibit preference for food items over tangible items and skew results of such intermixed assessments.

 

 

Caregiver Report:

Sometimes, the most useful information regarding preference can be gleaned from those who know the individual best. Asking caregivers informally, or by following a formal checklist, such as the RAISD, can be useful at identifying preferred stimuli.

 

 

Paired Stimulus Preference Assessments:

A paired choice preference assessment involves the presentation of 2 items at a time from a larger list (usually 7 - 12 items) to determine which items are the most preferred. Each item is presented in combination with every item on the list, so that the individual is given an opportunity to "choose" which item they like the most in a contest against every other item.

Often times, behavior analysts will ensure that the position (on the left, or on the right) of the various stimuli is evenly rotated to ensure that the individual is not just "choosing the item on the right side" (or exhibiting some other kind of position bias).

Food items are typically not intermixed with tangible items during preference assessments, as research suggests that some individuals may exhibit preference for food items over tangible items and skew results of such intermixed assessments.

 

 

Free Operant Preference Assessments:

A free operant preference assessment allows learners freedom to roam an area, such as a play room, and interact with any items in the room they find motivating. The duration of engagement is recorded for each item, allowing analysts to compare the amount of time the individual spent with each item, and therefore determine if one item was more "valuable" than another simply by comparing the quantity of time the individual allocated to interacting with one item(s) over other(s).

Typically, these rooms are "seeded" with likely high-preference items based off care-giver / parent / guardian report, which increases the likelihood of the assessment being successful at generating a hierarchy (or ranking) of preferred items.

fields.text: A multiple stimulus without replacement is described best by which of the following?
fields.hint:
A preference assessment allows us to determine what stimuli are (and are not) preferred by an individual, by measure of how much time they spend interacting with an item (or the frequency of times they choose that item from an array of other items).

 

PLEASE NOTE: preference for a stimulus (like M&Ms) does not necessarily imply that it will reinforce a contingent behavior! Reinforcer assessments are conducted when you need to demonstrate that a stimulus does have reinforcing value - preference assessments are typically done first to identify likely reinforcers.

Some big things to remember:

  1. Things that you generally "prefer" to interact with in your free time (like, say, watching Netflix, Hulu, whatever) aren't the only reinforcers for behavior. For example, chapstick is a reinforcer (for the behavior of putting chapstick on my lips) but only when the EO (chapped lips) is present. Similarly, kleenex is a reinforcer (for the behavior of reaching for / buying / kleenex) but only when the EO (a runny nose) is present.
  2. A powerful reinforcer (coffee, ice cream, netflix - I'm a simple man) may not be sufficient when the contingency is too demanding. For example, I will engage in high rates of "button pushing" to contact those items (uber eats; typing on a keyboard to find a show to watch; etc.). I will not engage in high rates of "mowing the lawn of a football sized field" to contact those reinforcers, however.

E.G. You offer me a plate with $1.00, a skittle, an M&M, and a smiley face sticker on it.

Each time I would probably choose the $1.00. You might write down "$1.00 is the most preferred item" and then attempt to use it as a reinforcer for a variety of tasks. If one of the tasks was touching my nose, sure, I'd be likely to find that $1.00 very reinforcing for that behavior. However, if you change the response requirement to "building a brick house" I am unlikely engage in very high rates of "house-building" behavior when the contingency is $1.00. My motivating operations will be changed by the response requirement, in this case! So keep that in mind when utilizing the results of your preferrence assessments.

Similarly, states of satiation and deprivation may alter the value of stimuli. Tokens, such as a $1.00, can be exchange for a great many reinforcers, which makes it hard to satiate on them. However, if I was only offerred food items during a reinforcer assessment, and you determined my #1, #2, and #3 favorite foods accurately, and then tried to use those items as reinforcers after I ate a big meal at lunch... you'd probably get a lot less behavior out of me. Motivation matters!

 

There are many types of preference assssments - here are the different types:

 

Trial Based Preference Assessments

Sometimes, behavior analysts will conduct formal preference assessments using the discrete-trial methodology: presenting a formal antecedent, expecting a response - in this case, a selection, and consequating that response with access to the selected stimulus. What follows are preference assessments in the "trial-based" format:

 

Multiple Stimulus WITH Replacement

A multiple stimulus with replacement preference assessment involves the presentation of typically 5 - 7 items at a time to determine which items are the most preferred and allow you to identify what is the "most valuable" item(s) from the array. Typically, one item will stand out from it's peers in the array - such as a special toy, like a blankie, or the iPad, etc. - that the individual will choose each and every time they are given the option to. Knowing what this stimulus is on a day-to-day basis can make these types of preference assessments incredibly valuable, especially for learners who have difficulty communicating their choice.

It's best practice for behavior analysts to rotate the position of each item in the array to ensure that the individual is not just "choosing the item on the right side" (or exhibiting some other kind of position bias).

Food items are typically not intermixed with tangible items during preference assessments, as research suggests that some individuals may exhibit preference for food items over tangible items and skew results of such intermixed assessments.

 

Multiple Stimulus WITHOUT Replacement (MSWO):

A multiple stimulus without replacement (MSWO - yes, I know, the acronym MSWO is missing the "r" so that's confusing!) preference assessment involves the presentation of typically 5 - 7 items at a time to determine which items are the most preferred and create a hierarchy of those items. Since the items are not "replaced", when the item is selected, it's gone for the remainder of that assessment, so typically the highest value items are selected first. This assessment is often repeated several times to determine the average "rank" of each item in the array.

It's best practice for behavior analysts to rotate the position of each item in the array to ensure that the individual is not just "choosing the item on the right side" (or exhibiting some other kind of position bias).

Food items are typically not intermixed with tangible items during preference assessments, as research suggests that some individuals may exhibit preference for food items over tangible items and skew results of such intermixed assessments.

 

Asking the Individual:

Caregiver Report:

Sometimes, the most useful information regarding preference can be gleaned from those who know the individual best. Asking caregivers informally, or by following a formal checklist, such as the RAISD, can be useful at identifying preferred stimuli.

 

Pre-Trial / Post-Trial Choice:

Sometimes, an individual's preferences change rapidly, or may change as a result of performing a task. For example, my preference for water before exercise might be low, but following exercise, might be very high. Because of this variability, some behavior analysts will ask before or after the demand so that the individual can select the item in that instant, based off their motivation in that moment.

 

 

Paired Stimulus Preference Assessments:

A paired choice preference assessment involves the presentation of 2 items at a time from a larger list (usually 7 - 12 items) to determine which items are the most preferred. Each item is presented in combination with every item on the list, so that the individual is given an opportunity to "choose" which item they like the most in a contest against every other item.

Often times, behavior analysts will ensure that the position (on the left, or on the right) of the various stimuli is evenly rotated to ensure that the individual is not just "choosing the item on the right side" (or exhibiting some other kind of position bias).

Food items are typically not intermixed with tangible items during preference assessments, as research suggests that some individuals may exhibit preference for food items over tangible items and skew results of such intermixed assessments.

 

 

Free Operant Preference Assessments:

A free operant preference assessment allows learners freedom to roam an area, such as a play room, and interact with any items in the room they find motivating. The duration of engagement is recorded for each item, allowing analysts to compare the amount of time the individual spent with each item, and therefore determine if one item was more "valuable" than another simply by comparing the quantity of time the individual allocated to interacting with one item(s) over other(s).

There are two basic "types" of free operant arrangements:

Contrived:

Typically, during a contrived free-operant assessment, these rooms are either "seeded" with likely high-preference items based off care-giver / parent / guardian report, which increases the likelihood of the assessment being successful at generating a hierarchy (or ranking) of preferred items.

Naturalistic:

In this arrangement, the individual is observed where they typically spend most of their free or "leisure" time to identify how they allocate their responding.

fields.text: Which of the following is an objective, concise, clear and complete response definition?
fields.hint:
Response definitions (also known as operational definitions) typically meet the following criteria:

  1. Objective - the behavior is described in terms that will likely cause any two observers to agree when the behavior did (or did not) occur; a.k.a. good inter-observer agreement, by following these rules:
    • Clear - the definition avoids vague or ambiguous language
    • Concise - the definition uses just enough language to convey the intended meaning
    • Complete - the definition encompasses all dimensions of the behavior of interest.

fields.text: Which of the following is a type of motivational variable that decreases the likelihood of behavior that produces a given stimulus as a consequence for that behavior (behavior-altering effect) AND decreases the effectiveness of that same given stimulus as a consequence (value-altering effect)?
fields.hint:
What are Motivating Operations?

Motivating Operations (MOs) are an environmental variable that have both an effect on the consequences for behavior, and the behavior itself. You've known about MOs all your life - you just probably used the more common parlance of "He likes ice cream," "I don't like Taylor Swift's music," or "I like to eat salsa." What you're talking about is the impact of a stimulus on your behavior, and you're sharing it so other people know that if they want to make themselves more reinforcing to you, they should have ice cream and salsa available when you come over, and leave Taylor Swift off the music playlist.

 

How do MOs work?

From a behaviorist's point of view, we must describe all stimuli in terms of the objective outcomes in terms of behavior change - this helps us avoid mentalistic descriptions which are outside the purvue of behavioral science.

 

Motivating operations (MOs) are linked to stimuli, and impact the organism in two ways:

1.  Value-altering effect: they modify (increase or decrease) the efficacy of a stimulus as a punisher or reinforcer

2.  Behavior-altering effect: they increase the frequency (increase or decrease) of a behavior that has been punished or reinforced by that stimulus.

 

For example, the sight of an empty gas guage while driving down the highway will increase the effectiveness of behaviors that produce gasoline as reinforcers (value-altering: increase), and increase the momentary frequency of behaviors that produce gasoline (behavior-altering: increase).

 

Other behaviors that will fill up your gas tank will also experience the same effect, proportional to their availability (as signaled by SDs) and their individual learning histories (of reinforcement, punishment). For example, maybe calling a roadside assistance service (such as AAA) or pulling over to the side of the road and sticking your thumb up.

 

Conversely, the sight of a full gas guage while driving down the road will decrease the effectiveness of behaviors that produce gasoline as reinforcers (value-altering: decrease), and decrease the momentary frequency of behaviors that might produce gasoline (behavior-altering: decrease).

 

 

EOs vs. AOs

It can be helpful to describe MOs more specifically when the need arises:

  • Establishing Operations (EOs) are motivating operations that establish (increase) the effectiveness of some stimulus as a reinforcer -- also establishing effect.

 

  • Abolishing Operations (AOs) are motivating operations that abolish (decrease) the effectiveness of some stimulus as a reinforcer -- also abative effect.

Of the choices below, which of the following best describes the scenario below?

An experimenter reduces the quantity of food provided for lab rats until their body weight is 80% below their baseline weight. In the future, when food is presented as a consequence for a given response (behavior), there is a momentary increase in their behavior (behavior-altering effect) and a momentary increase in the reinforcing value of food as a consequence for that same given response (value-altering effect).

fields.text:
Of the choices below, which of the following best describes the scenario below?

Typically, Sally-Mae rewards herself for hard work with ice cream every Thursday - however, today was a staff potluck at her place of work! There were mini-quesadillas, little pizza rolls, sandwiches, soups - it was, in a word, extravagant. She over indulged. After work, she found herself uninterested in driving (behavior-altering) to the local ice cream parlore like she typically does, and the thought of another bite to eat was just too much to bear (value-altering). She felt the gym calling her name.

fields.text: A differential reinforcement procedure where a specific behavior is placed on a higher schedule of reinforcement while other behaviors are placed on extinction (or less favorable schedules) is known as...?
fields.hint:
Differential Reinforcement of OTHER behavior (DRO) is the provision of reinforcement contingent upon any / all behaviors excluding a specific behavior. For example, you might provide a reinforcer every 5 minutes as long as a client has not engaged in aggressive behavior (hitting, kicking, slapping).

DROs may inadvertently reinforce undesired behaviors.

 

Differential Reinforcement of ALTERNATIVE behavior (DRA) is the provision of reinforcement contingent upon a specific behavior occurring. Typically, but not always, this is the same functional reinforcer as a behavior that might be simultaneously targeted for reduction.

Here's a link to an excellent video featuring Dr. Timothy Vollmer discussing differential reinforcement of alternative behavior, a research focus of his at his lab at the University of Florida.

fields.text: A differential reinforcement procedure where all behaviors EXCEPT one specific behavior are reinforced is referred to as...?

fields.text: A differential reinforcement procedure where the inter-trial interval is progressively expanded (increased) such that the overall rate of a behavior per unit of time has decreased is referred to as...?
fields.hint:
Differential Reinforcement of OTHER behavior (DRO) is the provision of reinforcement contingent upon any / all behaviors excluding a specific behavior. For example, you might provide a reinforcer every 5 minutes as long as a client has not engaged in aggressive behavior (hitting, kicking, slapping).

DROs may inadvertently reinforce undesired behaviors.

 

Differential Reinforcement of ALTERNATIVE behavior (DRA) is the provision of reinforcement contingent upon a specific behavior occurring. Typically, but not always, this is the same functional reinforcer as a behavior that might be simultaneously targeted for reduction.

Here's a link to an excellent video featuring Dr. Timothy Vollmer discussing differential reinforcement of alternative behavior, a research focus of his at his lab at the University of Florida.

 

Differential Reinforcement of HIGHER or LOWER rates of behavior (DRH / DRL) are both procedures that depend on the inter-trial interval of behavior, which might be a little confusing just looking at the name alone (i.e., the whole rate part). Yes, you are trying to reduce the rate of behavior, however responses are only reinforced if a specific latency has occurred since the last response. Therefore, you're really just trying to increase / decrease the inter-trial interval ("gap") between responses, which will, as a product, increase or decrease the rate, of course.

fields.text: The disruption of a previously reinforcing contingency, such that the functional reinforcer is no longer available, is referred to as?
fields.hint:
Extinction is the process of disrupting a previous reinforcing relationship such that a behavior that previously produced a given reinforcer no longer produces that reinforcer.

Extinction typically results in an extinction burst - a temporary increase in responding, prior to a usually sudden drop-off in behavior - as well as "emotional responding" aka "novel responding," which is the emergence of new topographies (or resurgence of previously extinguished behaviors that have produced the same functional reinforcer of the behavior currently on extinction).

fields.text: Tim, an RBT, is at the supermarket when he sees a client that he regularly works with. He excitedly greets his client and talks about their most recent therapy session. After he heads home, he realizes he did something wrong - what was it?
fields.hint:
The Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act has specific requirements for individuals who interact with Protect Health Information (PHI). 

 

Approaching a client in public and dicussing the details of a therapy session reveals two things: that the client is receiving therapy services, and may also reveal information about their diagnosis as well, both of which are protected elements of their medical record.

 

Tim would be advised to wait for the client to acknowledge him first, and then refrain from mentioning any details that might be classified as PHI. This can be very tricky thing to navigate in social contexts, such as a supermarket, mall, or community event, but is part and parcel of our obligation to protect the privacy of our clients as analysts.

fields.text:
Samantha is an RBT who works at a behavioral health clinic. She has just been put in charge of sending out notices to clients regarding special events coming up each week, but was not trained very well. At the start of this week, she sends a mass communication to all clients letting them know about a special Autism awareness event coming up that Friday. 

 

What did Samantha do wrong?
fields.hint:
The Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act has specific requirements for individuals who interact with Protect Health Information (PHI). Protected health information includes things like first / last names, medical records, etc. It is very important to handle this information carefully as the penalties imposed by the federal government are steep and there can be massive emotional / social consequences for clients who have had their data mishandled.

 

If you are responsible for client communications, you must send emails to multiple clients using the BCC option to protect their privacy. If you are unsure how to do this, you should not be in charge of sending out mass emails at your company! It is against federal law (HIPPA) to send information (such as email addresses) from one client to another without their explicit consent.

fields.text:
Sam is working with his supervisor and notices that his client is engaging in a novel form of self-injury. Unfortunately, his supervisor is not immediately available, so after resolving the situation to the best of his ability he attempts to notify his supervisor (via email).

 

Which of the following would be an objective, behavioral email to Sam's supervisor?
fields.hint:
It is important that all communications with supervisors be OBJECTIVE. A good test for objectivity is to ascertain if the message meets the following criteria:

  1. Is the message concise - is there a lot of unnecessary language / wordiness?
  2. Is the message clear -  is there any verbal ambiguity that could be resolved?
  3. Is the message complete - is there any information missing that is relevant to the issue at hand?

Additionally, it must be BEHAVIORAL - there must specific behavior mentioned, avoiding emotional / mentalistic terminology, e.g. "He got angry" would be better phrased as "He began to vocalize loudly for 30 - 45 seconds, repeatedly tapping his eye with his forefinger with enough pressure that damage could occur."

fields.text: Which of the following is an example of DISCONTINUOUS data collection?
fields.hint:
Remember:

  • Discontinuos data collection refers to data that is taken of some sample of the behavior, not each and every instance of the behavior of interest.
  • Continuous data collection refers to data that is taken on each and every instance of behavior.

The following are common types of DISCONTINUOUS data collection:

1. Momentary Time Sampling - recording data (YES or NO) regarding the occurrence of a behavior at a specific moment in time. This means that if the behavior was occurring for the entirety of the interval, but just happened to briefly stop at the point in time in which we observe the behavior, we might still mark 'no.' This is one of the obvious drawbacks of this data collection scheme. One of the up-sides is that it's relatively resource unintensive - a single data collector could easily take data on many individuals simultaneously without becoming too overloaded.

2. Partial Interval Recording - recording data (YES or NO) if the behavior occurs for any part of a given interval. For example, if the behavior occurs for 1 second or for the entire interval, you would still score it as a single "yes" for that interval. As a result, this type of recording tends to over-estimate behavior, which may be a good thing, depending on what you're trying to measure. For example, if you're teaching someone not to bite their teachers, even 1 second of biting could be pretty painful and disruptive. Therefore, you'd be happy with overestimation as it would help guide treatment decisions in the right direction.

3. Whole Interval Recording - recording data (YES or NO) if the behavior occurs for the ENTIRETY of an observation interval. For example, if the behavior occurs for 59 seconds out of a 60 second observation interval, you would not score that interval! That seems pretty arbitrary, but it has it's benefits - imagine a scenario where you are attempting to take data on many learners who are supposed to be working on independent work. These same learners must raise their hand if they'd like to get up from their table work. You could easily task a single teacher with taking WIR data on 5 or even 10 kids, and if you're interested in seeing an increase in their in-seat, on-task behavior, this would be a conservative measure of those behaviors -- a graph with a score of 100% would truly represent mastery, as even a single second of out-of-seat behavior would cost them an entire interval's score!

fields.text: What is considered "best practice" when it comes to updating graphs and collecting data regarding behaviors measured during the day?
fields.hint:
There are two basic rules about recording and charting data:

  • Always attempt to record data as soon as possible - if not as it occurs
    • If this is not possible, you should consider changing your data collection to something more feasible!

 

  • Charting (graphing) should be done either the same day, or at least once a week
    • You can use online data collection tools, such as CentralReach or Catalyst (and that's just 2 among many great choices) to automatically graph your data as you collect it!

 

You should always make your best effort to record data as it happens. To do this most effectively, one can use clickers, an app on a smart phone, or some other mechanical / digital tool to store data for you. If you work with clients who exhibit high frequency (or dangerous) behaviors, it can be challenging to provide for their safety while maintaining their safety and your safety.

fields.text:
Tilda finished her session after being supervised by her BCBA. During the session, she recorded data on a paper data collection sheet. While she was cleaning up, she spilled a cup of coffee all over her data sheet, making it completely illegible.

What should Tilda do? Her company has strict policies regarding staff who fail to properly enter data at the end of a shift!
fields.hint:
ABA is a science, and any science is nothing without accurate, reliable, and valid data collection. Falsifying data is never acceptable, although there may be times when estimations are acceptable. However, we should always communicate with our supervisors and colleagues when errors or mishaps occur that preclude accurate data collection, and no behavior analyst or registered behavior tech should ever falisify or misrepresent data collected during a session. Such an action would be a breach of our ethical code and bely the scientific foundation of our field.

Tilda should notify her supervisor of the issue and perhaps her company could consider switching to an electronic or mechanical data collection system (though those systems are not without their own weaknesses, such as power going out or a weak internet signal).

fields.text: When getting ready to collect behavior data, which of the following choices could be something you do to ensure you are well prepared and do a good job?
fields.hint:
Generally, you should do both of the following to be prepared to collect data during your session:

Rule #1 Be aware of what you are taking data on

  • What are your specific behaviors of interest? What are their response definitions?
  • What phases are each of your specific behaviors of interest in? (baseline, intervention, etc.)

 

Rule #2 Have your data collection tools ready!

  • If you are tracking several behaviors that may occur at high rates and / or simultaneously, are you ready for that?
  • Do you need clickers, a pad and paper, etc. to be able to take notes on behavior during your session
  • Your memory might be good, but you shouldn't rely on it

fields.text: When attempting to assess the function of a client's behavior, what is often considered the "gold standard" for experimentally identifying function?
fields.hint:
A functional analysis is an experimental methodology where an analyst repeatedly alters the contingencies in effect for a client's behavior in several test conditions with the goal of identifying which test condition is most reinforcing to the problem behavior. Since we know that a reinforcer increases a behavior over time, by repeatedly exposing behavior to putative reinforcers, we might expect to see an increase in that behavior over repeated exposures to the reinforcing test condition, and less or no change in the non-reinforcing test contingencies.

For example, some classic test contingenices are:

  • Attention - an adult pre-occupeis themselves with some activity and "ignores" the child, and attention is provided only contingent upon the behavior of interest occurring
  • Escape - demands are placed (typically academic, but they can be any type of demands) and escape is provided contingent upon the behavior of interest occurring
  • Control - the client receives attention and free access to high-value reinforcers. No additional consequence for the behavior of interest.
  • Alone - the client is left "alone" (i.e., in a room which has a few low to medium preference activities for them to engage in) and an adult pre-occupies themself with some other activity. No additional consequence for the behavior of interest.

There are many crucial ethical concerns to take into account when implementing a functional analysis, and informed consent of parents or caregivers is required. Sometimes, behaviors are too dangerous to conduct a functional analysis safely on - for instance, if a client engages in dangerous eye-gouging, exposing this behavior (eye-gouging) to reinforcement even briefly could be tremendously risky!

fields.text:
Sally is an RBT working with a client named Jim. Jim tends to scream and bite his arm forcefully when presented with his token board, and sometimes when Sally opens up her laptop. Sally almost never opens up her laptop unless she's about to ask Jim to do some of his table work activities.

What do you think the most likely function of Jim's behavior is?
fields.hint:
The client's behavior has a history of occuring in the presence of demands, or signals - such as the opening of a laptop - that demand might be imminent. Therefore, it is likely that Jim's behavior is maintained by escape from demand.

Sally might consider taking ABC data on Jim's SIB to see if a consistent pattern emerges. It may also be useful to conduct a functional analysis to formally demonstrate a relationship between demand and SIB if feasible and safe.

fields.text: From the four options below (multiple choice), which of the following choices are common environmental variables (antecedents) that may have impacted a client's learning during that session?
fields.hint:
Many things can impact a client's ability to learn during a session - sleep, illness, family life problems, medication changes - these are all things the board specifically mentions in the RBT task list (E-01). It's important to note these events when you are made aware of them and, as needed, report them to your supervisor so that each event can be documented.

Some families may change their child's medication on a day-to-day basis (even without approval from a child's pediatrician) and this can severely alter their behavior, as you would imagine. Sometimes, it is helpful to have a prepared script for the onset of your session, asking basic info about homeostatic variables (sleep, food), any significant episodes of challenging behavior that day, changes in medication, or events in the household that may impact the child's performance in your session.

Always remember to be respectful, too - some information may be uncomfortable or difficult for your client's parents or guardians to share.

fields.text:
When traveling between in-home therapy sessions, Todd accidentally forgot to store his client files and data sheets in the trunk of his car in the lockbox his company provides him. After a quick stop at a gas station, he found his car had been robbed, and his client files lost. Without knowing it, Todd has accidentally disclosed PHI and violated the Health Information Privacy & Portability Act.

 

What could Todd have done better to prevent this serious violation?
fields.hint: Your agency will be responsible for training you to the legal standard set by both local and federal law, per HIPPA. Generally, it is a very bad idea to leave PHI out and accessible by non-authorized individuals as it not only exposes your client(s) to vulnerability in the form of identity theft & violation of trust but it is also a serious crime!

fields.text: Which of the following way is a safe way to store data collected during a therapy session that may contain PHI (Personal Health Information)?
fields.hint:
Personal Health Information (PHI) - such as social security numbers, names, birthdays, diagnoses, treatment plan goals, etc. - must be kept in a locked (or password protected) file and comply with the standards set by the HIPPA act. From an RBT's perspective, you will likely be trained on a specific policy for your company, such as storing all client charts / data in binders in a lockable file cabinet or a locked room in your building.

When in doubt, contact your BCBA supervisor for specific advice on how to transport or store materials that contain PHI.

fields.text:
While working with a client with irritable bowel syndrome, Cassidy exclaims "ooooh-eeee! Somebody has the farts today!" in a joking tone. Her client is pretty much non-verbal, so it's not a big deal - it's not very likely they'll feel embarassed by farting a lot, or having people comment on their farts.

 

What's the most salient ethical dillema with Cassidy's behavior?
fields.hint:
As therapists, we must advocate for our clients. Part of that duty is respecting our client's dignity - providing them with the same privacy and respect we would want for ourselves. I imagine that Cassidy would be horrified if someone else loudly narrated any gastrointestinal distress she might experience throughout the day - and just because her client lacks the verbal skills necessary to indicate the punishing nature of her comments does not necessarily mean those comments are not functioning as punishers! The last thing we want to do, as therapists, is pair ourselves with punishment and become agents of aversiveness.

In addition, imagine how the parents might feel observing their child being treated this way. Would it nurture an environment of respect and trust? Probably not. Cassidy should discretely open a window but otherwise go about her day.

fields.text: Out of all of the options below, what is the RBT's role in the delivery of behavioral services (most closely)?
fields.hint:
The RBT primarily implements a behavior change plan, as designed by a certified analyst (BCaBA, BCBA). They are supervised regularly (5% of their direct hours) by a certified analyst to ensure competency. The RBT is on the front lines of behavioral service delivery - they work with clients, are trained to perform a wide variety of behavioral interventions, and collect (and may also graph) data on those interventions. The role of the RBT is pivotal when a BCBA or BCaBA is unavailable to work 1:1 with all of the clients on their caseload for all hours required in the service plan (which is often the case).

Please Note: RBTs - and BCaBAs, BCBAs, etc. - are not licensed - licensure is unique to each state in the U.S., and takes different shapes. Look up licensure in your state for more details. Some states don't offer licensure yet!

RBTs may know their clients better than their supervisors, and in some respects, even their parents - some clients may work with a single therapist 20 - 30 hours a week, every week. That's a lot of 1-on-1 time!

To ensure quality service delivery, the RBT is supervised for 5% of all hours worked in a service delivery period, and must pass a competency exam as well as a supervised observational period.

Wanna learn more? Read my earlier blog post for more on how folks can become an RBT:

https://aba.rocks/blog/so-you-want-to-become-an-rbt

fields.text: Prior to beginning a session, what is the minimum preparation required on your part, as an RBT / behavioral therapist?

  • What are your specific behaviors of interest? What are their response definitions?
  • What phases is each of your specific behavior(s) of interest in? (baseline, intervention, etc.)

 

Rule #2 Have your data collection tools ready!

  • If you are tracking several behaviors that may occur at high rates and/or simultaneously, are you ready for that?
  • Do you need clickers, a pad, and paper, etc. to be able to take notes on behavior during your session
  • Your memory might be good, but you shouldn't rely on it

fields.text: What's the difference between RATE and FREQUENCY in Applied Behavior Analysis?
fields.hint:
Answer: FREQUENCY refers to the total count of the behavior of interest, whereas RATE refers to the total count of the behavior per unit of time.

 

Historical Note:

2019 Update - historically, this question used to display a question that indicated that rate = frequency. This is a holdover from the 2014 task list, which used the terms interchangeably. As of 2019, the terms are now recognized as representing different things (rate = count of behavior per unit time, frequency = count of behavior, independent of time).

 

Citations:

Carr, J. E., Nosik, M. R. and Luke, M. M. (2018), On the use of the term ‘frequency’ in applied behavior analysis. Jnl of Applied Behav Analysis, 51: 436-439. doi:10.1002/jaba.449

fields.text: What are the THREE basic, measurable dimensional quantities of behavior?
fields.hint:
The THREE measurable dimensions of behavior are as follows:

  • Temporal Extent - the duration of the behavior can be measured from the onset (start) to the offset (offset)
  • Temporal Locus - behavior occurs at a POINT (locus) of time
  • Repeatability - behavior can be counted (once defined)

 

Source:

  • Cooper, John O., Heron, Timothy E.Heward, William L.. (2007) Applied behavior analysis /Upper Saddle River, N.J. : Pearson/Merrill-Prentice Hall,

fields.text:
Sam counts the number of times his sister picks her nose. He does this for 2 hours.

Later, for some peculiar reason, he divides the total count of nose-picking by the session length (in minutes).

What type of data is Sam calculating?
fields.hint:
Sam is calculating rate data - you can tell because he is measuring a behavior against some unit of time (in this case, the total count by the session length in minutes). This generates "rate per minute" data. 

More on rate below:

RATE is the total count of a behavior over time - for example, number of quiz questions completed in an hour, or number of widgets produced in a factory in a day. Rate is important because simply giving the count is often not enough to make a judgement about the behavior of interest - for example, if you wanted to drive the fastest car, you would want to know it's top speed in miles per hour as opposed to the mileage displayed on the odometer!

 

COUNT & FREQUENCY

Count = Frequency

Sometimes, you may encounter frequency and the term "count." In most (modern) cases, they mean the same thing. If you're a student going for your BCBA, you should read the historical note below because the term has an unfortunately murky, confusing past.

 

RATE VS. FREQUENCY  -  AN IMPORTANT DISTINCTION

Let's look at two examples of the same data, one measured in just frequency (count) vs. the same data, but converted to rate:

 

FREQUENCY (or total count) Data for 1 Week:

Table A
Session Day FREQUENCY aka COUNT Data
Monday 100
Tuesday 110
Wednesday 120
Thursday 130
Friday 140

 

RATE (aka, FREQUENCY) Data for 1 Week:

Table B
Session Day COUNT Data Session Length Calculation FREQUENCY / RATE
Monday 100 2 hours 100 / 2 hours 50 / hour
Tuesday 110 3 hours 110 / 3 hours 37 / hour
Wednesday 120 5 hours 120 / 5 hours 24 / hour
Thursday 130 7 hours 130 / 7 hours 19 / hour
Friday 140 8 hours 140 / 8 hours 18 / hour

 

As you can see, that's a big difference! The FREQUENCY (COUNT) data (table A) shows an increasing trend as the week goes on, and would be a cause for alarm if we were treating a problem behavior (or celebration if we were tracking some new, great skill).

However, when the FREQUENCY (COUNT) is converted into RATE we see a different, more accurate story. The client's week gets longer and longer as the week goes on, resulting in a pretty substantial decrease as time goes on (a little more than 50% decrease). Whether that's good or bad, of course, depends on whatever the behavior is, but you can see how if your client has different sessions, comparing FREQUENCY / COUNT to RATE can be very misleading and influence your judgement improperly! So be careful!

 

A Historical Note On Rate & Frequency

Frequency and Rate WERE considered synonymous in behavior analysis, as crazy as that might sound for those of you coming from backgrounds in other fields, such as mathematics or statistics. This has caused a lot of confusion. is In behavior analysis, RATE = FREQUENCY, at least at the time of this current writing, and likely for quite a long time after this, too.

In ABA, count is used to refer to the total number of occurrences of a behavior in a given period of time.

Frequency and Rate both refer to a count of behaviors over a unit of time. This is critical in behavioral observation as two sessions may have different lengths, causing visual analysis of graphs to be confounded.

 

 

Why did we have to use FREQUENCY = RATE? THAT'S MADNESS!

Why does the United States & England still not use the metric system? Why is pluto not a planet anymore? Why is coffee better than tea?

The answer is just simply culture and convention. If you read the Cooper, Heron, and Heward (2007) - largely considered THE textboo in behavior analysis, at least at the time of this writing in 2019 - you will likely encounter teaching that will shape your behavior to be in line with FREQUENCY = RATE. However, other texts (see the citations below) disagree, and think behavior analysts should change their mind. The BACB recently distinguished between frequency and rate on their 2019 task lists - thank god - but the confusion still remains, due to this historical naming convention.

Whatever happens in the future, I just hope we can keep it straight!

 

 

Sources:

  • Cooper, John O., Heron, Timothy E.Heward, William L.. (2007) Applied behavior analysis /Upper Saddle River, N.J. : Pearson/Merrill-Prentice Hall
  • Merbitz, C.T., Merbitz, N.H. & Pennypacker, H.S. On Terms: Frequency and Rate in Applied Behavior Analysis BEHAV ANALYST (2016) 39: 333. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40614-015-0048-z
  • Carr, James E., Nosik, Melissa R., Luke, Molli M. Journal of Applied Behavior Analysis (2018) 51(2):436-439. doi: 10.1002/jaba.449

fields.text: Which of the following is an adequate description of behavior, the nature phenomena that the study of behavior analysis focuses on?
fields.hint:
Behavior is the physical action of an organism which involves the movement of some part of that organism - be that it's vocal chords, synapses, or limbs. Single celled organisms exhibit behavior, as do multicellular organisms. Big animals exhibit behavior (whales), and so do small animals (rodents).

Behavior always involves some temporal locus (it happens at some point in time), temporal extent (it happens for a specific duration in time), and repeatability (it can be counted).

 

Sources:

  • Cooper, John O., Heron, Timothy E.Heward, William L.. (2007) Applied behavior analysis /Upper Saddle River, N.J. : Pearson/Merrill-Prentice Hall

 

"[behavior is] the interaction of the muscles and the glands of a live organism and the enviornment [the organism exists in at this moment]"

- Jack Michael

 

the behavior of an organism is that portion of an organism’s interaction with the environment that is characterized by detectable displacement in space through time of some part of the organism and that results in measurable change in at least one aspect of the environment
 
– Johnston & Pennypacker (1980, 1993a)

fields.text: What is a commonly used tool used by behavior analysts to identify an organism's preference value for a stimulus and the conditions under which that value might change when the contingency is modified (i.e., response effort, states of satiation / deprivation, or the schedule of reinforcement in effect)?
fields.hint:
A preference assessment allows us to determine what stimuli are (and are not) preferred by an individual, by measure of how much time they spend interacting with an item (or the frequency of times they choose that item from an array of other items).

 

PLEASE NOTE: preference for a stimulus (like M&Ms) does not necessarily imply that it will reinforce a contingent behavior! Reinforcer assessments are conducted when you need to demonstrate that a stimulus does have reinforcing value - preference assessments are typically done first to identify likely reinforcers.

Some big things to remember:

  1. Things that you generally "prefer" to interact with in your free time (like, say, watching Netflix, Hulu, whatever) aren't the only reinforcers for behavior. For example, chapstick is a reinforcer (for the behavior of putting chapstick on my lips) but only when the EO (chapped lips) is present. Similarly, kleenex is a reinforcer (for the behavior of reaching for / buying / kleenex) but only when the EO (a runny nose) is present.
  2. A powerful reinforcer (coffee, ice cream, netflix - I'm a simple man) may not be sufficient when the contingency is too demanding. For example, I will engage in high rates of "button pushing" to contact those items (uber eats; typing on a keyboard to find a show to watch; etc.). I will not engage in high rates of "mowing the lawn of a football sized field" to contact those reinforcers, however.

E.G. You offer me a plate with $1.00, a skittle, an M&M, and a smiley face sticker on it.

Each time I would probably choose the $1.00. You might write down "$1.00 is the most preferred item" and then attempt to use it as a reinforcer for a variety of tasks. If one of the tasks was touching my nose, sure, I'd be likely to find that $1.00 very reinforcing for that behavior. However, if you change the response requirement to "building a brick house" I am unlikely engage in very high rates of "house-building" behavior when the contingency is $1.00. My motivating operations will be changed by the response requirement, in this case! So keep that in mind when utilizing the results of your preferrence assessments.

Similarly, states of satiation and deprivation may alter the value of stimuli. Tokens, such as a $1.00, can be exchange for a great many reinforcers, which makes it hard to satiate on them. However, if I was only offerred food items during a reinforcer assessment, and you determined my #1, #2, and #3 favorite foods accurately, and then tried to use those items as reinforcers after I ate a big meal at lunch... you'd probably get a lot less behavior out of me. Motivation matters!

 

There are many types of preference assssments - here are the different types:

 

Multiple Stimulus WITH Replacement

A multiple stimulus with replacement preference assessment involves the presentation of typically 5 - 7 items at a time to determine which items are the most preferred and allow you to identify what is the "most valuable" item(s) from the array. Typically, one item will stand out from it's peers in the array - such as a special toy, like a blankie, or the iPad, etc. - that the individual will choose each and every time they are given the option to. Knowing what this stimulus is on a day-to-day basis can make these types of preference assessments incredibly valuable, especially for learners who have difficulty communicating their choice.

It's best practice for behavior analysts to rotate the position of each item in the array to ensure that the individual is not just "choosing the item on the right side" (or exhibiting some other kind of position bias).

Food items are typically not intermixed with tangible items during preference assessments, as research suggests that some individuals may exhibit preference for food items over tangible items and skew results of such intermixed assessments.

 

Multiple Stimulus WITHOUT Replacement (MSWO):

A multiple stimulus without replacement (MSWO - yes, I know, the acronym MSWO is missing the "r" so that's confusing!) preference assessment involves the presentation of typically 5 - 7 items at a time to determine which items are the most preferred and create a hierarchy of those items. Since the items are not "replaced", when the item is selected, it's gone for the remainder of that assessment, so typically the highest value items are selected first. This assessment is often repeated several times to determine the average "rank" of each item in the array.

It's best practice for behavior analysts to rotate the position of each item in the array to ensure that the individual is not just "choosing the item on the right side" (or exhibiting some other kind of position bias).

Food items are typically not intermixed with tangible items during preference assessments, as research suggests that some individuals may exhibit preference for food items over tangible items and skew results of such intermixed assessments.

 

 

Caregiver Report:

Sometimes, the most useful information regarding preference can be gleaned from those who know the individual best. Asking caregivers informally, or by following a formal checklist, such as the RAISD, can be useful at identifying preferred stimuli.

 

 

Paired Stimulus Preference Assessments:

A paired choice preference assessment involves the presentation of 2 items at a time from a larger list (usually 7 - 12 items) to determine which items are the most preferred. Each item is presented in combination with every item on the list, so that the individual is given an opportunity to "choose" which item they like the most in a contest against every other item.

Often times, behavior analysts will ensure that the position (on the left, or on the right) of the various stimuli is evenly rotated to ensure that the individual is not just "choosing the item on the right side" (or exhibiting some other kind of position bias).

Food items are typically not intermixed with tangible items during preference assessments, as research suggests that some individuals may exhibit preference for food items over tangible items and skew results of such intermixed assessments.

 

 

Free Operant Preference Assessments:

A free operant preference assessment allows learners freedom to roam an area, such as a play room, and interact with any items in the room they find motivating. The duration of engagement is recorded for each item, allowing analysts to compare the amount of time the individual spent with each item, and therefore determine if one item was more "valuable" than another simply by comparing the quantity of time the individual allocated to interacting with one item(s) over other(s).

Typically, these rooms are "seeded" with likely high-preference items based off care-giver / parent / guardian report, which increases the likelihood of the assessment being successful at generating a hierarchy (or ranking) of preferred items.

fields.text: What is one way to identify a person's preferences without using a direct assessment of preference, such as a trial-based preference assessment or free-operant based procedures?
fields.hint:
A preference assessment allows us to determine what stimuli are (and are not) preferred by an individual, by measure of how much time they spend interacting with an item (or the frequency of times they choose that item from an array of other items).

 

PLEASE NOTE: preference for a stimulus (like M&Ms) does not necessarily imply that it will reinforce a contingent behavior! Reinforcer assessments are conducted when you need to demonstrate that a stimulus does have reinforcing value - preference assessments are typically done first to identify likely reinforcers.

Some big things to remember:

  1. Things that you generally "prefer" to interact with in your free time (like, say, watching Netflix, Hulu, whatever) aren't the only reinforcers for behavior. For example, chapstick is a reinforcer (for the behavior of putting chapstick on my lips) but only when the EO (chapped lips) is present. Similarly, kleenex is a reinforcer (for the behavior of reaching for / buying / kleenex) but only when the EO (a runny nose) is present.
  2. A powerful reinforcer (coffee, ice cream, netflix - I'm a simple man) may not be sufficient when the contingency is too demanding. For example, I will engage in high rates of "button pushing" to contact those items (uber eats; typing on a keyboard to find a show to watch; etc.). I will not engage in high rates of "mowing the lawn of a football sized field" to contact those reinforcers, however.

E.G. You offer me a plate with $1.00, a skittle, an M&M, and a smiley face sticker on it.

Each time I would probably choose the $1.00. You might write down "$1.00 is the most preferred item" and then attempt to use it as a reinforcer for a variety of tasks. If one of the tasks was touching my nose, sure, I'd be likely to find that $1.00 very reinforcing for that behavior. However, if you change the response requirement to "building a brick house" I am unlikely engage in very high rates of "house-building" behavior when the contingency is $1.00. My motivating operations will be changed by the response requirement, in this case! So keep that in mind when utilizing the results of your preferrence assessments.

Similarly, states of satiation and deprivation may alter the value of stimuli. Tokens, such as a $1.00, can be exchange for a great many reinforcers, which makes it hard to satiate on them. However, if I was only offerred food items during a reinforcer assessment, and you determined my #1, #2, and #3 favorite foods accurately, and then tried to use those items as reinforcers after I ate a big meal at lunch... you'd probably get a lot less behavior out of me. Motivation matters!

 

There are many types of preference assssments - here are the different types:

 

Trial Based Preference Assessments

Sometimes, behavior analysts will conduct formal preference assessments using the discrete-trial methodology: presenting a formal antecedent, expecting a response - in this case, a selection, and consequating that response with access to the selected stimulus. What follows are preference assessments in the "trial-based" format:

 

Multiple Stimulus WITH Replacement

A multiple stimulus with replacement preference assessment involves the presentation of typically 5 - 7 items at a time to determine which items are the most preferred and allow you to identify what is the "most valuable" item(s) from the array. Typically, one item will stand out from it's peers in the array - such as a special toy, like a blankie, or the iPad, etc. - that the individual will choose each and every time they are given the option to. Knowing what this stimulus is on a day-to-day basis can make these types of preference assessments incredibly valuable, especially for learners who have difficulty communicating their choice.

It's best practice for behavior analysts to rotate the position of each item in the array to ensure that the individual is not just "choosing the item on the right side" (or exhibiting some other kind of position bias).

Food items are typically not intermixed with tangible items during preference assessments, as research suggests that some individuals may exhibit preference for food items over tangible items and skew results of such intermixed assessments.

 

Multiple Stimulus WITHOUT Replacement (MSWO):

A multiple stimulus without replacement (MSWO - yes, I know, the acronym MSWO is missing the "r" so that's confusing!) preference assessment involves the presentation of typically 5 - 7 items at a time to determine which items are the most preferred and create a hierarchy of those items. Since the items are not "replaced", when the item is selected, it's gone for the remainder of that assessment, so typically the highest value items are selected first. This assessment is often repeated several times to determine the average "rank" of each item in the array.

It's best practice for behavior analysts to rotate the position of each item in the array to ensure that the individual is not just "choosing the item on the right side" (or exhibiting some other kind of position bias).

Food items are typically not intermixed with tangible items during preference assessments, as research suggests that some individuals may exhibit preference for food items over tangible items and skew results of such intermixed assessments.

 

Asking the Individual:

Caregiver Report:

Sometimes, the most useful information regarding preference can be gleaned from those who know the individual best. Asking caregivers informally, or by following a formal checklist, such as the RAISD, can be useful at identifying preferred stimuli.

 

Pre-Trial / Post-Trial Choice:

Sometimes, an individual's preferences change rapidly, or may change as a result of performing a task. For example, my preference for water before exercise might be low, but following exercise, might be very high. Because of this variability, some behavior analysts will ask before or after the demand so that the individual can select the item in that instant, based off their motivation in that moment.

 

 

Paired Stimulus Preference Assessments:

A paired choice preference assessment involves the presentation of 2 items at a time from a larger list (usually 7 - 12 items) to determine which items are the most preferred. Each item is presented in combination with every item on the list, so that the individual is given an opportunity to "choose" which item they like the most in a contest against every other item.

Often times, behavior analysts will ensure that the position (on the left, or on the right) of the various stimuli is evenly rotated to ensure that the individual is not just "choosing the item on the right side" (or exhibiting some other kind of position bias).

Food items are typically not intermixed with tangible items during preference assessments, as research suggests that some individuals may exhibit preference for food items over tangible items and skew results of such intermixed assessments.

 

 

Free Operant Preference Assessments:

A free operant preference assessment allows learners freedom to roam an area, such as a play room, and interact with any items in the room they find motivating. The duration of engagement is recorded for each item, allowing analysts to compare the amount of time the individual spent with each item, and therefore determine if one item was more "valuable" than another simply by comparing the quantity of time the individual allocated to interacting with one item(s) over other(s).

There are two basic "types" of free operant arrangements:

Contrived:

Typically, during a contrived free-operant assessment, these rooms are either "seeded" with likely high-preference items based off care-giver / parent / guardian report, which increases the likelihood of the assessment being successful at generating a hierarchy (or ranking) of preferred items.

Naturalistic:

In this arrangement, the individual is observed where they typically spend most of their free or "leisure" time to identify how they allocate their responding.

 

Citations:

  • Cooper, John O., Heron, Timothy E.Heward, William L.. (2007) Applied behavior analysis /Upper Saddle River, N.J. : Pearson/Merrill-Prentice Hall
  • DeLeon, I. G., & Iwata, B. A. (1996). Evaluation of a multiple-stimulus presentation format for assessing reinforcer preferences. Journal of Applied Behavior Analysis, 29(4), 519–533. http://doi.org/10.1901/jaba.1996.29-519

fields.text: What is a developmental assessment?
fields.hint:
What follows are descriptions for various types of assessments - some assessments might meet all, some, or none of the criteria below. It is important to be familiar with these terms before using an assessment, so that you understand the implications of the assessment you are working with.

 

Developmental assessments assess skills based both on the individual’s chronological age (how old they actually are) versus how old they are in terms of the skills they have learned in contrast to the skills typically learned by that age. This is referred to as their “developmental age.” The goal for clinicians using a developmental assessment is to calculate the difference between the client’s chronological age and their developmental age, attempting to “close the gap” as quickly and efficiently as possible.

 

Criterion-based assessments involve presenting skills with specific criteria (an objective performance measure) that need to be mastered before the skill is considered mastered. These skills are typically organized into long-term goals, short-term goals, and instructional goals (from broader to narrow focus) for the convenience of the professional using the assessment. 

 

Curriculum-based assessments are assessments organized in a progressive manner, with suggestions and guides for progressing from one skill to the next as part of a coordinated curriculum. They give you examples of what to teach and in what order, and may also include teaching materials (such as worksheets, manipulative, sight word decks, etc.).

 

Social skills assessments directly target social behaviors and often require the presence of one or more (or even groups) of similarly skilled peers. This is one of the inherent limitations of a social skills program - if the client does not have access to an environment with similar peers from whom social behaviors can contact reinforcement, no social skills program will be effective. Social skills curricula typical emphasize skills such as verbal behavior, understanding body language, defining and interpreting emotions of yourself and others, and other similar behaviors that typically produce socially mediated reinforcers. This can also include some “a-social” skills, such as brushing your teeth or wearing deodorant, as these skills impact your relationships with others (being “stinky” might repel others). 

 

Norm-referenced assessments calculate a quotient score, which can be compared against a standard of deviation to determine where the user performs compared to other persons using the assessment. For example, a score of 100 is “average” and reflective of typical performance on that assessment by typical members of the population the assessment is designed for (i.e., school kids in the first grade, or children at the age of 5). A score of 120 would be above average, and a score of 80 would be below average.

fields.text: What is considered the gold standard in terms of identifying the "why" behind a behavior?
fields.hint:
A functional analysis is a type of functional assessment where consequences for problem behavior are manipulated in an alternating design to demonstrate which consequences are likely functional reinforcers for a given behavior.

It can be odd to conduct a functional analysis as the goal is unusual - from the onset, you are attempting to reinforce problem behavior. By testing multiple types of potential reinforcers, you identify what type of antecedents and consequences likely evoke and reinforce that problem behavior. Much like an allergy test involves exposing a patient to allergens to determine what you're allergic to, a functional analysis involves exposing problem behavior to the contingencies that maintain it to identify the "source" of the problem (i.e., the "allergen").

 

Citation(s):

Iwata, B. A., Dorsey, M. F., Slifer, K. J., Bauman, K. E., & Richman, G. S. (1994). Toward a functional analysis of self-injury. Journal of Applied Behavior Analysis, 27(2), 197–209. http://doi.org/10.1901/jaba.1994.27-197

Cooper, John O., Heron, Timothy E.Heward, William L.. (2007) Applied behavior analysis /Upper Saddle River, N.J. : Pearson/Merrill-Prentice Hall,

fields.text: Which of the following types of assessments identifies the maintaining reinforcer for a given behavior?
fields.hint:
A functional analysis is a type of functional assessment where consequences for problem behavior are manipulated in an alternating design to demonstrate which consequences are likely functional reinforcers for a given behavior.

It can be odd to conduct a functional analysis as the goal is unusual - from the onset, you are attempting to reinforce problem behavior. By testing multiple types of potential reinforcers, you identify what type of antecedents and consequences likely evoke and reinforce that problem behavior. Much like an allergy test involves exposing a patient to allergens to determine what you're allergic to, a functional analysis involves exposing problem behavior to the contingencies that maintain it to identify the "source" of the problem (i.e., the "allergen").

 

There are 3 general methods for identifying function:

Indirect Assessments - these are rating scales, questionnaires, checklists, and even informal interviews where caregivers or the client themselves are consulted. During this time, the analyst is asking questions regarding antecedents and consequences with the hope of identifying a pattern which will lead them to the behavior's function.

Descriptive Assessments - these are observational assessments that do not involve making changes to the environment (typically).

  • ABC Data involves collecting information regarding the changes in the environment immediately prior to a behavior
  • Scatterplot Analysis involved identifying the time that a behavior occurs, in order to identify if there is a pattern (for example, the behavior only happens from 1:00pm - 1:30pm, or only happens on Tuesdays and Thursdays)

Functional Analyses - there are multiple types of functional analysis, all of which involve modifying antecedent and / or consequent responses in the environment to identify if the behavior increases in certain conditions. It would follow that if a reinforcer is made contingent upon a behavior, the behavior will increase (that is the definition of a reinforcer, after all). That reinforcer is the function of the behavior.

 

Citation(s):

Iwata, B. A., Dorsey, M. F., Slifer, K. J., Bauman, K. E., & Richman, G. S. (1994). Toward a functional analysis of self-injury. Journal of Applied Behavior Analysis, 27(2), 197–209. http://doi.org/10.1901/jaba.1994.27-197

fields.text: What type of design is employed by a functional analysis to verify the maintaining variables of a given behavior?
fields.hint:
A functional analysis is a type of functional assessment where consequences for problem behavior are manipulated in an experimental*, alternating design to demonstrate which consequences are likely functional reinforcers for a given behavior.

** Note - in the context of behavior analysis, "experimental" does not necessarily mean "untested" or "unproven." The word experimental indicates that the analyst is verifying a functional relationship.

It can be odd to conduct a functional analysis as the goal is unusual - from the onset, you are attempting to reinforce problem behavior. By testing multiple types of potential reinforcers, you identify what type of antecedents and consequences likely evoke and reinforce that problem behavior. Much like an allergy test involves exposing a patient to allergens to determine what you're allergic to, a functional analysis involves exposing problem behavior to the contingencies that maintain it to identify the "source" of the problem (i.e., the "allergen").

fields.text: While writing a mass email to all the patients at the behavior analysis clinic she works at, Sam cc (carbon copies)  all of the families receiving services. What, if any, is the issue with this?
fields.hint:
The Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act has specific requirements for individuals who interact with Protect Health Information (PHI). Sharing protected health information is strictly prohibited; violating this policy can incur hefty fines as well as cost you your job. In addition, sharing protected information can irreperably damage an individual's trust with you and behavior analysis as a field - or even other mental health / service providers. This can cause an individual to forgo potentially life-altering treatment because of a silly, avoidable mistake. It's your responsibility to protect the privacy and dignity of every individual you serve.

 

Sam should use the bcc option (blind carbon copy) because the carbon copy option allows other recipients of the email to identify other patients at her clinic.

fields.text:
A little boy is playing with his toys in his room. Holding one of his stuffed animal dolls, he looks at it and says "Zebra!"

Which elementary verbal operant does this scenario most likely describe?
fields.hint:
A tact is labeling a non-verbal stimulus (i.e., not written words). Tacts are maintained by generalized social reinforcement (i.e., interaction / attention from others as a response to your tacting behavior).

In this scenario, the boy is labeling something seen in his environment.

fields.text:
A child sees a cookie and says "cookie." Without any knowledge of the child's motivation, what type of verbal operant does this most closely describe?

Be careful - this is a trick question!
fields.hint:
Tacts vs. Mands:

In real life, most verbal behavior is not "pure" - that is to say, it is under the control of multiple variables. When a child sees a cookie, they may say "cookie" as a tact (they are labeling the cookie) or as a mand (they want to eat the cookie) or, frankly, as both! Generally speaking, most of our verbal behavior is under multiple control like this.

For this question, as we are specifically not told the learner's MO, we are unsure if a mand is occurring. We must remember (and watch out for!) trick questions or tricky scenarios like this. Mands are only mands if there is a MO present. For the purposes of studying for an exam, most examples will be "pure" elementary operants like this.

fields.text:
A child sees a pizza box and says "pizza." Without any knowledge of the child's motivation, what type of verbal operant does this most closely describe?

Be careful - the child is seeing a pizza box, but we don't know if they want a pizza, if they're hungry/full, etc. You are distinguishing between tact and mand in this question - understandably, some people find this question a little tricky when these concepts are initially presented. You've got this!

fields.text:
It's right before lunch, and Sally is riding in the car with her mother. They pass her favorite fast food restaurant and Sally says "Mom, can we get a burger? I'm starving!" In this case, assume that Sally has an MO for a burger of some kind.

 

What type of verbal operant does this most closely resemble?
fields.hint:
A mand is a verbal operant that is under the control of a MO (motivating operation). A "pure" mand occurs soley and spontaneously in the presence of the MO; however, a tact-mand can occur (i.e., you see / smell something yummy and then mand for the stimulus that corresponds to the tact).

Organisms with verbal behavior will only mand in a state of deprivation (i.e., they have not had access to the stimulus for some length of time). I will not mand for ice cream after eating so much that I feel like my stomach might burst (this is called satiation). However, I will mand for it on a hot day after having had nothing to eat for quite some time (depriviation).

A quick way to tell if a mand is a mand is to identify motivation - if there's no evidence of motivation, no mand is probably happening.

fields.text: Who wrote the book Verbal Behavior and famously founded Radical Behaviorism, a forerunner to what would eventually be Applied Behavior Analysis?
fields.hint:
B.F. Skinner was the pioneer who founded radical behaviorism, which can be distinguished from the methodological behaviorism that preceded it by it's inclusion of thinking, feeling, and other private events in the analysis of animal behaviors.

Some of the concepts to emerge from Skinner's work include:

  • The cumulative record
  • The S-R-S contingency or Operant Conditioning
  • The "Skinner Box" (or Operant Chamber)
