fields.text: What is discrimination training?
fields.hint:
The Good Kind of Discrimination

So, the word discrimination usually conjures up images of racism, sexism, or any other kind of bad -ism. But in the world of behavior analysis, discrimination is a fundamental operant (skill) that is necessary in almost everything we do.

A basic discrimination is emitting a behavior in the presence of a stimulus, and not emitting that behavior in it's absence. This is a basic kind of discrimination.

A more complex discrimination might be stopping at a red light, and driving at a green light. Two stimuli either evoke or abate a behavior (driving), and the learner's history of consequences for behavior in the presence of those stimuli control it (avoiding accidents and tickets for running a red light; being able to get to your destination for driving following the green light).

The sheer quantity of discriminations that must be made on a daily basis is overwhelming, and for those who are unable to make conditional discriminations, serves as a substantial handicap. For this reason, discrimination training is a critical component of any skill acquisition program where it has been identified as a deficit.

fields.text:
An unleared functional relationship between the wetness / dryness of an environment and the speed of movement (irrespective of direction) is exhibited by the wood louse. The dryer it is, the more it moves (in any particular direction); the wetter it is, the slower the wood louse moves.

What type of selectionism is likely most responsible for this behavior?
fields.hint:
Change

Time

 

The gradual change over time of organisms occurs due to constant interaction between that organism and the environment. Selectionism is the term for the perpetuation of traits that are helpful to the organism in some fashion with the removal of traits that are unhelpful. Selectionism is classically understood in the frame of gene expression, but also occurs with behavior.

Selectionism of behavior occurs at three levels:

  • Phylogeny - biology of the organism
  • Ontogeny - the learning history of the organism
  • Cultural - meta-contingencies produced by groups of socially interacting organisms

In Skinner's 1968 work, Selection by Consequences, the parallels between natural selection and operant selection by consequences were illuminated. The process by which behavior is selected and maintained is very similar to the process by which genetic code mutates and is then naturally selected by the environment. From the abstract of Skinner's article:

Selection by consequences is a causal mode found only in living things, or in machines made by living things. It was first recognized in natural selection, but it also accounts for the shaping and maintenance of the behavior of the individual and the evolution of cultures. In al three of these fields, it replaces explanations based on the causal modes of classical mechanics. The replacement is strongly resisted. Natural selection has now made its case, but similar delays in recognizing the role of selection in the other fields could deprive us of valuable help in solving the problems which confront us.

Selection by Consequences - B.F. Skinner, 1968

 

A Warning:

In each of the sections below, I will identify and describe the three levels of selection as reported by Skinner. Nature abhors a vacuum (horror vacui), so much so that it should be easy for us to remember that nothing ever happens in one.

The sexual behavior of humans, for example, is sometimes hotly debated. How much is nature, and how much is nurture, and can an understanding be predictive of the overt sexual behavior? Some claim that gender is purely a social construct, while others claim that your behavior is the product of cultural norms that are shared by members of groups and subgroups. Both camps will often indicate that your genes are involved to some degree. This is, essentially, an argument of "nature vs. nurture," with refinements on nurture to include societies, cities, and families.

The behavior analyst knows better. We know that sexual behavior involves synaptic activation, hormone release, reflexes, and other processes. These processes interact with other variables: the individual organism has a genetic endowment that predisposes certain stimuli to have an antecedent evocative effect, and predisposes other stimuli to function as reinforcers and punishers. The organism' behavior will, of course, be shaped (learned) in the environment it lives in, producing change, however malleable. The culture will also exert change on the organism to a degree as well, resulting in contingencies on the individual as well as meta-contingencies as products of the group's behavior.

In short, all levels of selectionism occur continuously. One level of selection is insufficient to explain the organism - the phylogenic, ontogenic, and cultural levels of selection will exhibit selection pressure constantly, and result in change in behavioral repertoires.

 

 

Phylogeny

The phylogeny of an organism refers to "the evolutionary development and diversification of a species or group of organisms, or of a particular feature of an organism." In behavior analysis, the focus is on overt behavior - therefore, we will limit ourselves to biological change (i.e., mutations) that result in changes in dimensions of reflex behavior or the function of antecedent stimuli in the environment (or internal stimuli, such as private events, states of deprivation, or gestation of offspring). Do not discount that, simultaneously, mutations may result in physiological difference (e.g., new fur colors, suppression of gene expression resulting in the loss of a trait, or gaining the superpowers of the X-men).

What follows are mostly examples of reflexes are derived in part from Jack Michael's Concepts & Principles, an excellent textbook that all behavior analysts should read thoroughly and perhaps more than once (if you are like me). All of the following enable the organism to survive more efficiently through the process of selectionism.

Examples of Phylogenic Reflexes:

Tropism - an unlearned behavior where an organism (typically a plant) will orient or grow in the direction of an unconditioned stimulus, such as a source of light. Tropism is sometimes selected for in organisms where a stimulus is scarce and competition is fierce; e.g., in a forest, phototropism is the process by which trees, shrubs, and other plants grow in the direction of light, an important resource for plants. Some forms of tropism, such as geotropism (differential growth in the direction of gravitational forces), do not involve competition but instead convey direct survival value to the organism through more efficient resource transport (maybe through capillary action facilitated by gravity, more efficient use of extant hydraulic distribution systems, etc.)

Kinesis - unlearned change in movement speed of an organism elicited by an unconditioned stimulus; the change in movement is irrespective of direction. The movement of the wood louse increases in dry places and decreases in damp places - damp places are where more of it's nutrients are available. This enables the "lucky" wood louse to remain in wet, favorable environments, and, should it stumble away from them, it will "speed up" and likely return to the original or speedily move to a new wet spot.

Taxis - unlearned change directional movement. The movement may be towards or away from a stimulus. For example, positive phototaxis is movement towards a source of light (moths) and negative phototaxis is movement away from a source of light (e.g., the fruit fly instar avoid bright places).

Fixed Action Pattern - a rigid sequence of responses evoked by an environmental stimulus or internal condition). Once started, the fixed action pattern continues to occur, invariantly, and without change even with regard to the effect of additional responses on the environment. Examples can include egg retrieval by some geese, nest-weaving by some species of spiders, and mating and aggressive behavior in male stickleback fish. The unconditioned stimulus that evokes the fixed action pattern is sometimes referred to as a "super-stimulus" or "releaser" by ethnologists; the fixed action pattern is also sometimes referred to as a modal action pattern.

Adaptation - sensory organs change / reduce their sensitivity to a continuous, unchanging stimulus. The activation threshold for the rods / cones in the eye in terms of synaptic firing to the efferent nerve will vary based off the environment's varying light. During the bright daylight hours, a high level of stimulation (light) is required for efferent nerve activation. You may spend a long time indoors (say, at a movie theater) and then, upon leaving, experience the unpleasant sensation as your eyes "adjust" to the new brightness. This is adaptation. At night, a lower threshold is required, and your eyes will gradually adjust to the lower level of sensitivity required to function. A temporary flash of light - say, from a flashlight - may cause temporary "night blindness" whereupon your eyes will adapt in the wrong direction due to the presence of the errant flashlight beam.

 

 

Ontogeny

The ontogeny of an organism refers to the individual learning history, with operant behavior being selected by the consequences that behavior produces in the environment. Learning is the story of an organism' ontogeny: lasting, but not permanent, changes in the organism' behavior through the interaction that behavior produces in the environment (consequences).

Taking your trash out in Saturdays may be beneficial in some cities where the garbage collection occurs early on Sunday mornings. However, if that individual were to move to another city, the environment would change and so too might the contingency. Perhaps trash is taken out on Thursdays in this new environment, and the old behavior of taking the trash out on Saturdays results in positive punishment in the form of reprimands and chiding from concerned neighbors who don't enjoy the site of the garbage bins on the side of the street for half the week at a time. Quickly, the behavior is likely to change. It may change even faster if the individual is a compulsive rule-follower (has a strong history of reinforcement for identifying and following rules) and seeks out the rule after the move.

Another example: the behavior of speaking Japanese in Japan produces more reinforcement in that environment, but may produce less reinforcement in some rural areas of the United States. Therefore it is not surprising that we observe more individuals speaking Japanese in Japan than in rural areas of the United States. The consequences of such behavior shape the repertoire of an individual over time; as the environment changes, so too will the behavioral repertoire of an organism.

 

Some Examples of Types of Learning:

Habituation - an unconditioned stimulus produces a reflex response, such as jumping at a loud noise or salivation at the presentation of a food item. Repeated presentation results in a gradual reduction in responding, which will return to baseline levels after a period of time expires. When I worked at a tex-mex restaurant for many years, the sight of chopped vegetables, spicy salsa, cooking meats, etc. produced a salivation response. At the onset of a shift, salivation occurred. As the shift progressed, I salivated less and less at the sight of the food I worked with nearly continuously throughout the shift. Changes in state of food deprivation are being ignored for the purposes of this example, but surely played a role as well. When I was younger, I would play scary video games, like Silent Hill or Resident Evil. The scariest "scares" always came at the beginning of the play session, when I first bumped into something scary. Sometimes, I would visibly jump out of my seat - but as the gaming session went out, I would become fairly calm and the visible "jump" response would deteriorate to nothing. Then I'd take a break for pizza, maybe my Mom would coerce me into doing some chores, and finally, some time later, I'd return to the game and immediately jump at something that I had been previously habituated to.

Respondent Conditioning - a neutral stimulus reliably precedes an unconditioned stimulus for a reflex response (see the examples above under Phylogeny). Over time, if the temporal distance between the neutral stimulus and the unconditioned stimulus is short enough (say, a few seconds at most), the neutral stimulus will acquire the same function as the unconditioned stimulus in terms of eliciting the reflex. Respondent conditioning occurs all the time, and may be a useful part of advertising - the successful grocery store places the deli and bakery at the entrance of the store, pairing walking into the store with sweet or savory smelling foods, eliciting salivation and establishing the value of food as a consequence for behavior. Of course, the grocer sells food, and now may notice increases in profits when the bakery and deli are open and cooking vs. when they are closed and no savory aromas are emanating from their respective locations. The Grocer may go one step further and place their logo in a place of prominence by the deli, bakery, or by "sample" stations, such that the visual stimulus is paired with the presentation of an unconditioned stimulus (in this case, yummy food). Over time, the effect may be to cause the reflex response (salivation) in the presence of the previously neutral, but now conditioned, eliciting stimulus (the store's logo). It's god damn maniacal, and writing this has left me hankering for a pub sub. Clever manipulation of environmental contingencies is the most effective advertisement.

Operant Conditioning - antecedent stimuli precede a behavior, which may have a value or behavior-altering effect. The behavior occurs and produces a consequence. That consequence, which may have been previously established (or abolished) in value by antecedent variables, will alter the future frequency of that behavior to some degree. This is the classic "A - B - C" contingency: antecedent → behavior → consequence. This sequence deserves it's own article, and has been the focus of study in the applied literature since the instantiation of applied behavioral science.

 

 

Cultural

It is easy to overlook the impact of cultural selection on human behavior as a behavior analyst, but to do so would be foolish. Cultures are an emergent property of social interaction between organisms. As Sigrid Glenn said in her 1988 paper in The Behavior Analyst titled Contingencies & Meta-Contingencies: Toward a Synthesis of Behavior Analysis and Cultural Materials (quite a mouthful):

"... DNA replication made biological evolution possible and operant behavior made cultural evolution possible."

Individual behavior serves as the basis from which contingencies of reinforcement emerge and produce what we describe as cultural practices. For example, in the United States, individual contingencies operate on the red and green light system at traffic lights. A driver stops at the red light, and drives when the green light is displayed. Some individuals do not follow this rule 100% of the time, especially in south Florida, but the vast majority follow the rule. The individual contingencies are simpler: getting to your destination safely, avoiding tickets, etc. A meta-contingency emerges: as drivers obey this system, they reach their destination more efficiently (faster time). While being stopped at a red light is certainly dreadful when you are in a rush, imagine the scenario without the light: individuals may compete for passage, beeping their horns and swerving through traffic to make it to their destination. If you don't think this would be the outcome, you have another think coming: watch this video if you need proof. The usage of the traffic light system to promote individual safety has the functional effect of optimizing traffic, or at least creating the opportunity for city planners to optimize traffic (not to imply that they do - at least not in my city. But it certainly is possible).

The cultural level of selection is the most important level for the future of human life on Earth. At this time, we are producing more toxins and pollution than we can safely process. We are consuming more food than we need to feed ourselves, while many go hungry and die. We do this because individual contingencies are taking precedence over cultural meta-contingencies. We must shape our society to save our future. In time, I hope that a corps of behavioral engineers is able to help design law and policy with these contingencies in mind. We may be able to build ourselves a better life, but save our future from ourselves.

Over time, a mutation occurs in a particular species of plant, causing a chemical (known as auxin) to result in differential elongation of cells, which is inhibited in the presence of light and invigorated in its absence. In short, all levels of selectionism occur continuously. One level of selection is insufficient to explain the organism - the phylogenic, ontogenic, and cultural levels of selection will exhibit selection pressure constantly, and result in a change in behavioral repertoires.

 

 

Phylogeny

The phylogeny of an organism refers to "the evolutionary development and diversification of a species or group of organisms, or of a particular feature of an organism." In behavior analysis, the focus is on overt behavior - therefore, we will limit ourselves to biological change (i.e., mutations) that result in changes in dimensions of reflex behavior or the function of antecedent stimuli in the environment (or internal stimuli, such as private events, states of deprivation, or gestation of offspring). Do not discount that, simultaneously, mutations may result in physiological difference (e.g., new fur colors, suppression of gene expression resulting in the loss of a trait, or gaining the superpowers of the X-men).

What follows are mostly examples of reflexes are derived in part from Jack Michael's Concepts & Principles, an excellent textbook that all behavior analysts should read thoroughly and perhaps more than once (if you are like me). All of the following enables the organism to survive more efficiently through the process of selectionism.

Examples of Phylogenic Reflexes:

Tropism - an unlearned behavior where an organism (typically a plant) will orient or grow in the direction of an unconditioned stimulus, such as a source of light. Tropism is sometimes selected for in organisms where a stimulus is scarce and competition is fierce; e.g., in a forest, phototropism is the process by which trees, shrubs, and other plants grow in the direction of light, an important resource for plants. Some forms of tropism, such as geotropism (differential growth in the direction of gravitational forces), do not involve competition but instead convey direct survival value to the organism through more efficient resource transport (maybe through capillary action facilitated by gravity, more efficient use of extant hydraulic distribution systems, etc.)

Kinesis - unlearned change in movement speed of an organism elicited by an unconditioned stimulus; the change in movement is irrespective of direction. The movement of the woodlouse increases in dry places and decreases in damp places - damp places are where more of its nutrients are available. This enables the "lucky" woodlouse to remain in wet, favorable environments, and, should it stumble away from them, it will "speed up" and likely return to the original or speedily move to a new wet spot.

Taxis - unlearned change directional movement. The movement may be towards or away from a stimulus. For example, positive phototaxis is the movement towards a source of light (moths) and negative phototaxis is the movement away from a source of light (e.g., the fruit fly instar avoid bright places).

Fixed Action Pattern - a rigid sequence of responses evoked by an environmental stimulus or internal condition). Once started, the fixed action pattern continues to occur, invariantly, and without change even with regard to the effect of additional responses on the environment. Examples can include egg retrieval by some geese, nest-weaving by some species of spiders, and mating and aggressive behavior in male stickleback fish. The unconditioned stimulus that evokes the fixed action pattern is sometimes referred to as a "super-stimulus" or "releaser" by ethnologists; the fixed action pattern is also sometimes referred to as a modal action pattern.

Adaptation - sensory organs change/reduce their sensitivity to a continuous, unchanging stimulus. The activation threshold for the rods/cones in the eye in terms of synaptic firing to the efferent nerve will vary based on the environment's varying light. During the bright daylight hours, a high level of stimulation (light) is required for efferent nerve activation. You may spend a long time indoors (say, at a movie theater) and then, upon leaving, experience the unpleasant sensation as your eyes "adjust" to the new brightness. This is adaptation. At night, a lower threshold is required, and your eyes will gradually adjust to the lower level of sensitivity required to function. A temporary flash of light - say, from a flashlight - may cause temporary "night blindness" whereupon your eyes will adapt in the wrong direction due to the presence of the errant flashlight beam.

Learning is the story of an organism' ontogeny: lasting, but not permanent, changes in the organism' behavior through the interaction that behavior produces in the environment (consequences).

Taking your trash out in Saturdays may be beneficial in some cities where the garbage collection occurs early on Sunday mornings. However, if that individual were to move to another city, the environment would change and so too might the contingency. Perhaps trash is taken out on Thursdays in this new environment, and the old behavior of taking the trash out on Saturdays results in positive punishment in the form of reprimands and chiding from concerned neighbors who don't enjoy the site of the garbage bins on the side of the street for half the week at a time. Habituation - an unconditioned stimulus produces a reflex response, such as jumping at a loud noise or salivation at the presentation of a food item. Repeated presentation results in a gradual reduction in responding, which will return to baseline levels after a period of time expires. When I worked at a tex-mex restaurant for many years, the sight of chopped vegetables, spicy salsa, cooking meats, etc. produced a salivation response. At the onset of a shift, salivation occurred. As the shift progressed, I salivated less and less at the sight of the food I worked with nearly continuously throughout the shift. Changes in the state of food deprivation are being ignored for the purposes of this example, but surely played a role as well. When I was younger, I would play scary video games, like Silent Hill or Resident Evil. The scariest "scares" always came at the beginning of the play session, when I first bumped into something scary. Sometimes, I would visibly jump out of my seat - but as the gaming session went out, I would become fairly calm and the visible "jump" response would deteriorate to nothing. Respondent Conditioning - a neutral stimulus reliably precedes an unconditioned stimulus for a reflex response (see the examples above under Phylogeny). Respondent conditioning occurs all the time and maybe a useful part of advertising - the successful grocery store places the deli and bakery at the entrance of the store, pairing walking into the store with sweet or savory smelling foods, eliciting salivation and establishing the value of food as a consequence for behavior. Of course, the grocer sells food and now may notice increases in profits when the bakery and deli are open and cooking vs. when they are closed and no savory aromas are emanating from their respective locations. The Grocer may go one step further and place their logo in a place of prominence by the deli, bakery, or by "sample" stations, such that the visual stimulus is paired with the presentation of an unconditioned stimulus (in this case, yummy food). Over time, the effect may be to cause the reflex response (salivation) in the presence of the previously neutral but now conditioned, eliciting stimulus (the store's logo). It's god damn maniacal, and writing this has left me hankering for a Pub-Sub. Clever manipulation of environmental contingencies is the most effective advertisement.

Operant Conditioning - antecedent stimuli precede a behavior, which may have a value or behavior-altering effect. The behavior occurs and produces a consequence. That consequence, which may have been previously established (or abolished) in value by antecedent variables, will alter the future frequency of that behavior to some degree. This is the classic "A - B - C" contingency: antecedent → behavior → consequence. This sequence deserves it's own article, and has been the focus of study in the applied literature since the instantiation of applied behavioral science.

It is easy to overlook the impact of cultural selection on human behavior as a behavior analyst, but to do so would be foolish. Cultures are an emergent property of social interaction between organisms. As Sigrid Glenn said in her 1988 paper in The Behavior Analyst titled Contingencies & Meta-Contingencies: Toward a Synthesis of Behavior Analysis and Cultural Materials (quite a mouthful):

"... DNA replication made biological evolution possible and operant behavior made cultural evolution possible."

While being stopped at a red light is certainly dreadful when you are in a rush, imagine the scenario without the light: individuals may compete for passage, beeping their horns and swerving through traffic to make it to their destination. If you don't think this would be the outcome, you have another think coming: watch this video if you need proof. The usage of the traffic light system to promote individual safety has the functional effect of optimizing traffic or at least creating the opportunity for city planners to optimize traffic (not to imply that they do - at least not in my city. We are consuming more food than we need to feed ourselves, while many go hungry and die. We do this because individual contingencies are taking precedence over cultural meta-contingencies. We must shape our society to save our future. In time, I hope that a corps of behavioral engineers are able to help design law and policy with these contingencies in mind. We may be able to build ourselves a better life but save our future from ourselves.

fields.text: Which of the following best describes determinism, one of the basic principles of behavior analysis?
fields.hint:
"Science is first of all a set of attitudes."

B.F. Skinner, 1953

The behavior of scientists is as important as the subjects they study. Public and private events that a person engages in can be used to identify whether their behavior is scientific or not-scientific. The following behaviors have been identified as fundamental to successful scientific behavior, and are not exclusive to behavior analysis.

 

Determinism

The interaction of phenomena in the universe follows stable, immutable and basic laws. Every result has a cause. While it may be infeasible (or even impossible due to computational limits at present), a system can be analyzed and modeled such that any output (result) can be determined to have one set of input(s) (causes). In the end, as strange as they may be, functional relationships between certain phenomena and other phenomena produce a certain result, all other things considered.

 

Empiricism

Direct, objective observation of phenomena, without bias, prejudice, or personal opinion. Your results should be observable by anyone else who chooses to replicate and your empirical methodology, as your results are based on a verifiable truth which anyone else with the right tools can corroborate.

 

The basic strategy of science is to take a hypothesis and demonstrate a functional relationship between two variables: the dependent variable and the independent variable. The test is commonly called an experiment, and the methodology should be as empirical as possible (objective + clearly described so that others can replicate it). Experiments must be carefully designed so as to eliminate as many extraneous variables as possible, which could prevent the results from being interpreted.

 

Parsimony

All simple, logical explanations of the behavior should be ruled out before entertaining more complex solutions. This is similar to Occam's Razor, a "law" of sorts that states, "One should not increase, beyond what is necessary, the number of entities required to explain anything." The good behavior analyst should agree - don't overcomplicate things!

 

Pragmatism

"Consider the practical effects of the objects of your conception. Then, your conception of those effects is the whole of your conception of the object."

Charles Sanders Peirce, The Pragmatic Maxim

Functional relationships between variables are valued over the creation of representations or hypothetical constructs. Avoiding the generation of meta-physical theories and explanations and instead focusing on a science grounded on human experience and behavior. The role of the scientist is to clarify and refine mankind's understanding of natural processes surrounding us, and not to create layers of abstraction that might serve as explanatory fictions or mentalisms. The purpose of science is to elucidate truth, not to obfuscate it.

Your results should be observable by anyone else who chooses to replicate and your empirical methodology, as your results are based on a verifiable truth which anyone else with the right tools can corroborate.

 

The basic strategy of science is to take a hypothesis and demonstrate a functional relationship between two variables: the dependent variable and the independent variable. The test is commonly called an experiment, and the methodology should be as empirical as possible (objective + clearly described so that others can replicate it). Experiments must be carefully designed so as to eliminate as many extraneous variables as possible, which could prevent the results from being interpreted.

 

Parsimony

All simple, logical explanations of the behavior should be ruled out before entertaining more complex solutions. This is similar to Occam's Razor, a "law" of sorts that states, "One should not increase, beyond what is necessary, the number of entities required to explain anything." The good behavior analyst should agree - don't overcomplicate things!

 

Pragmatism

"Consider the practical effects of the objects of your conception. Then, your conception of those effects is the whole of your conception of the object."

Charles Sanders Peirce, The Pragmatic Maxim

Functional relationships between variables are valued over the creation of representations or hypothetical constructs. Avoiding the generation of meta-physical theories and explanations and instead focusing on a science grounded on human experience and behavior. The role of the scientist is to clarify and refine mankind's understanding of natural processes surrounding us, and not to create layers of abstraction that might serve as explanatory fictions or mentalisms. The purpose of science is to elucidate truth, not to obfuscate it.

fields.text: Which of the following best describes empiricism?
fields.hint:
"Science is first of all a set of attitudes."

B.F. Skinner, 1953

The behavior of scientists is as important as the subjects they study. Public and private events that a person engages in can be used to identify whether their behavior is scientific or not-scientific. The following behaviors have been identified as fundamental to successful scientific behavior, and are not exclusive to behavior analysis.

 

Determinism

The interaction of phenomena in the universe follows stable, immutable and basic laws. Every result has a cause. While it may be infeasible (or even impossible due to computational limits at present), a system can be analyzed and modeled such that any output (result) can be determined to have one set of input(s) (causes). fields.text: True or False: in Behavior Analysis, the terms "count" and "rate" mean the same thing.
fields.hint:
Count = Frequency

False - Count and and Rate DO NOT are not the same!

 

A quick terminology refresher:

  • Count - total number of instances of a behavior, also called frequency.
  • Rate - the amount of behavior per unit time

 

Citations:

Carr, J. E., Nosik, M. R. and Luke, M. M. (2018), On the use of the term ‘frequency’ in applied behavior analysis. Jnl of Applied Behav Analysis, 51: 436-439. doi:10.1002/jaba.449

fields.text: In Behavior Analysis, are the terms "count" and "frequency" synonymous (they mean the same thing)?
fields.hint:
True - count and frequency are synonyms!

 

A quick terminology refresher:

  • Count - total number of instances of a behavior, also called frequency.
  • Rate - the amount of behavior per unit time

 

Citations:

Carr, J. E., Nosik, M. R. and Luke, M. M. (2018), On the use of the term ‘frequency’ in applied behavior analysis. Jnl of Applied Behav Analysis, 51: 436-439. doi:10.1002/jaba.449

fields.text: In Behavior Analysis, are the terms "RATE" and "FREQUENCY" synonymous (they mean the same thing)?
fields.hint:
False. Rate does not equal frequency (at least, not anymore! - this used to be subject of contention in behavior analysis. Rate used to equal frequency for historical reasons in the field of behavior analysis, and this was a source of great confusion.)

  • Rate is the amount of behavior occurring per some unit of time, such as widgets produced at a factory or hats made by a milliner.
  • Frequency is just the amount of a behavior - also known as the total "count."

 

Citations:

 

Carr, J. E., Nosik, M. R. and Luke, M. M. (2018), On the use of the term ‘frequency’ in applied behavior analysis. Jnl of Applied Behav Analysis, 51: 436-439. doi:10.1002/jaba.449

fields.text: Which of the following is a measure of temporal extent?
fields.hint: Duration measures temporal extent - that is to say, how much time a behavior lasts. Typically, an onset and offset will be defined to make operationalizing a response easier.

fields.text: A user of the cell phone comes to expect that when a certain light is blinking on their phone, they have an unread text message. Assuming they find text messages reinforcing in terms of the behavior of checking their cell phone's text messages, the blinking light could be best conceptualized as a...?
fields.hint: A discriminative stimulus, or SD, is a stimulus that correlates with the availability of reinforcement for a specific behavior.

fields.text:
A child is learning to make a sandwich from a parent. The parent teaches each step, one step at a time, prompting their child when they make a mistake.

Each step in the process of making the sandwich serves as both the SD for the next step, and reinforcer for the completion of the previous step. What type of teaching process does this most resemble?
fields.hint: A task-analyzed behavior chain is a series of discrete behaviors where each behavior's completion serves as a reinforcer for the previous step and the SD for the next step in the chain. The terminal step produces the ultimate, back-up reinforcer as a product of completion of the task. Examples include tying your shoes, making a sandwich, following a YouTube tutorial to program a website built on Django / Python, or washing your hands.

fields.text:
A behavior repeatedly contacts the same consequence. That behavior increases over time.

 

What type of consequence does this most closely resemble?
fields.hint:
Reinforcement is the process by which a behavior increases over some unit of time. The unit of time is very important - you cannot say that a behavior "was reinforced" after just one exposure of that behavior to a consequence. After several exposures, however, you can describe an increasing trend through data collection -- i.e., an increase in rate / minute, an increase in total frequency per day, etc.

Beware statements like "I reinforced him with an M&M" or "is chocolate a reinforcer?" -- those are insufficient to understand any situation. A behavior must be measured over time to describe a reinforcement operation.

Be careful about this - people love this common, tricky question!

fields.text: Which of the following are essential components that must be understood before you teach a skill acquisition program?
fields.hint:
The following are example of essential components of a skill acquisition program:

  • Materials - what items, if any, are needed to complete the program.
  • Long Term Goal (or, Long Term Objective) - typically achieved in a six to twelve month time frame, with a broad and general statement such as “student will read sight words at the 2nd grade level” or “student will be able to prepare, consume, and put away snack materials without going off task.” A long term goal (LTG) will generate several suitable short term goals, which allow you to focus treatment decisions and begin to identify discrete behaviors for that skill that might need to be taught.
  • Short Term Goal (or, Short Term Objective) - typically achieved on the time frame of a few weeks to a few months, short term goals are collections of specific related skills that support the long term goal. Continuing the example above with a long term goal of “student will read sight words at the 2nd grade level,” some examples of supporting short term goals could include identifying letters printed in a variety of fonts, mastering 50 sight words, and decoding unknown words using phonics.
  • Learn Unit - “The learn unit consists of the inter-locking operants of instruction that incorporate particular student and teacher interactions that predict whether student behavior will be controlled by particular stimuli and setting events.” (Greer, 1994a). This is a description, essentially, of how to teach (and respond to) the behavior of a learner. You will typically encounter this in the form of a written “ABC” (antecedent, behavior, consequences) for the skill being taught.
    • Response Definition - Objective description of the target behavior
    • Antecedent - the MOs, SDs, and any other setup that needs to be arranged prior to the behavior occurring
    • Consequence - typically, the teacher/interventionists response, usually providing a specifically prescribed reinforcer or punisher differential to the “correctness” of the learner’s response.

 

Sources:

Long term goals and objectives:

  • Schloss, P. J. & Smith; J. A. (1998). Applied Behavioral Analysis in the Classroom (2nd ed.). Boston: Allyn & Bacon.

 

The Learn Unit

  • Greer, R. D., & McDonough, S. H. (1999). Is the learn unit a fundamental measure of pedagogy? The Behavior Analyst, 22(1), 5–16.

fields.text: When a behavior maintains across time and occurs in all desired contexts, it is said to have...?
fields.hint:
Train and hope was described by T.F Stokes and Donald Baer as:

“After a behavior change is effected through manipulation of some response consequences, any existent generalization across responses, settings, experimenters, and time, is concurrently and/or subsequently documented or noted, but not actively pursued.”

 

What does this mean?

Some analysts fall into the trap of simply “hoping” that generalization will occur without actively programming for it - as described in their original article, there are at least 7 suggested methods by which an analyst can actively promote generalization of a skill across time, people, and places.

  1. Sequential Modification - when transferring stimulus control from one setting to another, allow for small successive approximations from the initial comntrolling stimulus to progressively different variations of the stimulus until, eventually, the dimensions of the SD have been altered sufficiently and the terminal stimulus has effective control of the target behavior. 
  2. Introduce to Natural Maintaining Contingencies - plan to fade any artificially dense schedule of reinforcement towards the active schedule in the client’s natural environment.
  3. Train Sufficient Exemplars - introduce the learner to sufficient variants of the target stimuli such that reinforcement has been contacted for engaging in the response when a wide variety of non-critical elements of the SD / relevant dimensions for stimulus transfer have been varied or removed - i.e., tacting “bird” when shown a variety of birds of different colors, shapes, sizes (all non-critical elements of the class of animal) whereas some features will likely be consistent across all exemplars (has wings, a beak, feathers, etc.)
  4. Train Loosely - little or no effort is made to control (in an experimental / highly consistent manner) the presentation of the stimuli and the range of acceptable answers is broadened.
  5. Use Indiscriminable Contingencies - during teaching, use or fade towards intermittent schedules of reinforcement to mirror the likely schedule(s) that will be encountered naturalistically. Additionally, if necessary, make it hard to determine when the behavior will contact reinforcement and when it will not, to promote responding even in contexts where reinforcement is not likely to occur.
  6. Program Common Stimuli - plan to use stimuli that are relevant to the learner and will likely be encountered in the day-to-day natural environment. For example, if you are teaching the child tacts, teach them first things they see on their daily routine - their lunchbox, a doorknob, a car, etc.
  7. Mediating Generalization - establishing a sufficiently broad response when learning a new skill that it is likely to be employed in other types of skills - i.e., a child who is being taught how to cut on a dashed line to make animal cut-outs allows a learner to cut out different shapes of animals, which may include untrained exemplars.
  8. Train to Generalize - consider generalization itself an operant that can be reinforced. When the learner engages in novel generalized behavior, provide reinforcement for that behavior (or differential reinforcement for approximations of generalized responding).

fields.text:
A therapist used a physical prompt to evoke a response on trial #1. On trials #2, #3, and #4 she continues to use physical prompts. On trial #5, she uses a model prompt, and on subsequent trials, she uses a delayed model prompt. On each trial, she is attempting to reduce the support she is providing and differentially reinforces the student's responding as it occurs.

Of the choices below, which teaching strategy is most closely described above?
fields.hint: Prompt fading is the process of reducing prompting in a systematic fashion. Therapists provide prompts with the goal of reducing and eventually eliminating them as they reinforce a desired response. Prompt fading can involve reducing a response prompt (such as physical prompting) or gradually eliminating a stimulus prompt (such as slowly removing a bright color card behind the correct answer in an array).

fields.text: Which verbal operant involves a person perceiving some non-verbal stimulation in the environment (such as a color, or an airplane) and is maintained by general social reinforcement?
fields.hint:
A tact is under the antecedent control of non-verbal stimuli, and is reinforced by general social reinforcement. A tact can be visual (you see it), but it can also be olfactory (you smell it) or proprioceptive (your sense of position & movement in space).

An example of a tact could be a 2-year old child looking at an airplane and saying "an airplane in the sky" with a sense of aw and wonder that often escapes us adults, who have come to take for granted that millions of people regularly fly around in little tin cans every single day.

fields.text:
Elizabeth is working for a child who has been making tremendous progress. The client's birthday is coming up, and Elizabeth has some money saved up! She decides to buy her client a used iPad for his birthday -- this will be mostly useful not just as really fancy toy, but also as a teaching tool when she is there for therapy sessions.

 

What ethical consideration(s) is/are relevant here?
fields.hint:
RBT 2.04 - RBTs do not accept gifts or give gifts to clients.

 

Unfortunately for Elizabeth, while her intentions are good, it is an ethical violation to give her client a gift (even more so when the gift is substantial, such as a new and expensive tablet). Gift giving can create dual relationships and conflicts of interest that put her professional relationship with her client in danger. Elizabeth should avoid giving gifts to her client -- instead, maybe she could make a list of birthday wishes for her client's parents, who might be eager for gift ideas for their child.

fields.text:
A client makes a "gift" for her favorite RBT, Luisa, giving her a handmade card with macaroni noodles on it. Luisa politely and calmly refuses the gift, as the RBT Ethics code specifically bans RBTs accepting gifts from clients.

 

What ethical consideration, if any, is applicable here?
fields.hint:
RBT 2.04 - RBTs do not accept gifts or give gifts to clients.

In this case, Luisa should accept the gift as it has no "street value." Generally speaking, RBTs should be aware of the code item specified above, RBT 2.04 - RBTs do not accept gifts or give gifts to clients. In some cases, such as this one, where the gift is hand-made and of no appreciable value, accepting the gift will not harm the therapeutic relationship and is acceptable.

 

When making considerations regarding whether to accept a gift or not, RBTs must be exceptionally careful. Many (if not most) times, the RBT should simply ask the client to allow them time to ask their supervisor. However, in situations where the RBT is comfortable with the ethics code and understands that the gift has 0 monetary value, they may choose to accept the gift to prevent damaging rapport with their client. 

 

In some cultures, it would be damaging to therapeutic rapport to refuse items that could otherwise be considered as "gifts" - whenever possible, explain to the family that the board explicitly forbids accepting gifts to ensure protection of clients and therapists from the formation of conflicts of interest and potentially exploitative relationships.

In some circumstances, this may not be possible. For example, if a child gives you a "gift" in the form of a paper drawing / handmade card ("no street value", and thus unlikely to cause a dual relationship) -- in such a case, the RBT might be behaving in a rude manner and offend the family by strictly following the BACB's policy. Accepting such handmade, no-value gifts would not be an ethical violation. However, accepting car repair services from the client's mother, who happens to be a mechanic, would be an ethical violation.

In some cultures, refusing offered beverages or food may be insulting, and damage the therapeutic relationship. The analyst and any supervised RBTs must carefully weight the ethical requirement of the ethics code against the cultural practices of their clients and choose the best course of action carefully.

In these circumstances, it is advised that the RBT consult their supervisor if they encounter situations that fall into these gray areas, and act in accordance with the supervisor's feedback.

 

Got an ethics question? Don't hesitate to call the ABA Ethics Hotline, for free! More information is available at their website:

  • https://www.abaethicshotline.com/who-we-are/

fields.text:
An experienced RBT supervises other RBTs at work, due to a shortage of board certified assistant (BCaBA) and board-certified behavior analysts (BCBAs).

What, if any, ethical consideration exists here?
fields.hint: 3.01 RBTs only practice under the close, ongoing supervision of a qualified supervisor.

fields.text: An RBT unwittingly commits an ethical violation when working at a clinic. Who is liable for this breach of conduct?
fields.hint: RBTs are required to be knowledgeable of the RBT Ethics code. Ignorance of the code does not excuse ethical violations.

fields.text:
An RBT working with a client is asked by the parent to perform a functional analysis that the BCBA on the case had planned to do, but, due to an unexpected emergency, has to delay by a week.

Since the BCBA on the case is unavailable at the time, and the RBT is in school working toward their BCBA certification, the parent wants to proceed with the RBT implementing the functional analysis. The caregiver has taken some time to look up and research functional analysis procedures on the internet in order to provide support. Together, they feel confident that they can perform the functional analysis without the help of the BCBA.

The parent urges the RBT to help her because her child’s behavior is getting worse every passing day.

 

What should the RBT do?
fields.hint:
RBT Ethics Code 3.02 - RBTs follow the direction of their supervisors and inform them when they are asked to do something that goes beyond the scope of their certification.

 

RBTs must always be aware of their scope of competency. The task list is not a comprehensive; the RBT must always be competent with the population they serve. For example, an RBT working with a geriatric population would not be competent to work with a population of early learners with autism. Additionally, RBTs must be certain not to breach the scope of their skill competency, even when they are working with a familiar population. An RBT is not competent to perform a functional analysis - only an adequately trained BCBA is permitted to supervise and conduct a functional analysis. RBTs must be aware of their skill competency limitations, and act accordingly.

fields.text:
Tim, an RBT, usually works with early intervention clients in the 2 - 3 year age range whom all have a diagnosis of autism or developmental delay. After a few months, the clinic he works at begins to accept new clients who are aged 12 - 14, are all members of a state sponsored foster care program, and have an excellent array of verbal skills and no diagnosis of autism.Tim has never worked with this population before, but is excited by the challenge and opportunity to help these kids.

What should Tim do?
fields.hint:
RBT Ethics Code 3.04 - RBTs may not practice with new client populations without proper training and oversight.

 

The RBT must restrict their work to populations they are trained to work with, and with whom they have (and continue to receive) regular supervision from a board certified behavior analyst while they are providing behavioral therapy. This ensures the RBT provides competent care with respect to the unique challenges and considerations that may be endemic to groups of people who may request behavioral intervention, such as children with autism, individuals with traumatic brain injury, or persons who have developmental disability.

fields.text:
To make ends meet, Bethany works two jobs - one as an occupational therapist (OT), and the other part-time as an RBT at another clinic. While working as an OT, she begins to implement behavior change procedures based off the principles of applied behavior analysis without the supervision of a BCBA and advertises her status as a registered behavior therapist to her clients, which is outside of her job role at that specific job.

What, if anything, is wrong with this scenario?
fields.hint:
The most relevant ethical code consideration is as follows:

RBT Ethics Code 3.08 - If RBTs are involved in the delivery of non-behavior-analytic interventions, they do not make reference to, display, or otherwise use their RBT in that practice.

Bethany should avoid advertising her RBT credential unless she meets the criteria for it's use, which is specified by the BACB in the RBT task list and ethics code. Specifically, Bethany should obtain the ongoing supervision of a BCBA before implementing behavior analytic interventions with any client, refrain from making behavioral (but not occupational therapy) treatment decisions when working at her OT job, and avoid advertising herself as an RBT.

fields.text:
Maria, a BCBA, sends the "raw" results (just the spreadsheet scores) of the VB-MAPP behavioral assessment that the parents of her 24-year-old client, Sam, had previously consented to. The parents of Sam are his legal guardians, as Sam had previously been adjudicated incompetent, and Sam's parents are currently his legal guardians. When sending the family the assessment results, she does not accompany this with any further analysis or interpretation.

What, if any, ethical consideration is relevant here per the BACB's ethics code?
fields.hint:
The behavior analyst must explain assessment results adequately to consumers. This includes utilizing appropriate, easily understood graphic displays to represent any data collected / progress monitoring, and present this information to the client such that it can be understood.

  • The behavior analyst should avoid sending raw or uninterpreted assessment results to clients
  • The behavior analyst should avoid using technical jargon
  • The behavior analyst should avoid asking leading questions when checking understanding - ask open-ended questions to identify it he consumer or consumer's guardian understands the information presented

 

3.04 Explaining Assessment Results

  • Behavior analysts explain assessment results using language and graphic displays of data that are reasonably understandable to the client.

fields.text: Unless otherwise indicated by your local jurisdiction, how long are behavior analysts required to keep and maintain their professional records?
fields.hint:
Unless you are otherwise required to do so (e.g., state laws), you must maintain your records for a minimum of 7 years.

 

2.11 Records and Data

  1. Behavior analysts create, maintain, disseminate, store, retain, and dispose of records and data relating to their research, practice, and other work in accordance with applicable laws, regulations,and policies; in a manner that permits compliance with the requirements of this Code; and in a manner that allows for appropriate transition of service oversight at any moment in time.

  2. Behavior analysts must retain records and data for at least seven (7) years and as otherwise required by law.

  3.  

2.07 Maintaining Records

  1. Behavior analysts maintain appropriate confidentiality in creating, storing, accessing, transferring,and disposing of records under their control, whether these are written, automated, electronic, or in any other medium.

  2. Behavior analysts must retain records and data for at least seven (7) years and as otherwise required by law.

fields.text: The BACB's Ethical Code ("Code") describes the standards for obtaining permission for video or auditory recordings, such as recording an interview or service delivery during a session, in which of the following sections of the Code?
fields.hint:
The client must be informed when an electronic recording of an interview takes place. This is pertinent to audio recordings (e.g., using a microphone, smartphone, etc.) or a video recording (video camera, security camera, smartphone, etc.).

Permissions must be obtained prior to recording and use-cases must be specified; permission must be obtained for each use-case you may desire, e.g. for training purposes for future staff, to present at conferences, to share with other families, etc.

Please note this is specific to recording and usages of recording. This question is fairly tricky, because this is not apropos to similar but distinct code elements relevant to disclosing information to others, maintaining confidentiality, keeping records, 3rd party consultation, etc. Keep this in mind as small changes in wording changes everything, sometimes, and this is an important skill to have when taking tests!

 

2.05 Rights and Prerogatives of Clients

  1. The rights of the client are paramount and behavior analysts support clients’ legal rights and prerogatives.

  2. Clients and supervisees must be provided, on request, an accurate and current set of the behavior analyst’s credentials.

  3. Permission for electronic recording of interviews and service delivery sessions is secured from clients and relevant staff in all relevant settings. Consent for different uses must be obtained specifically and separately.

  4. Clients and supervisees must be informed of their rights and about procedures to lodge complaints about professional practices of behavior analysts with the employer, appropriate authorities, and the BACB.

  5. Behavior analysts comply with any requirements for criminal background checks.

fields.text: What types of activities WILL COUNT towards your restricted hours requirement (formerly known as indirect hours) in pursuit of your BCBA supervised experience hours?
fields.hint:
As of 2018, the following activities are described by the board (from the BACB's website, accessed May 2019):

  • Observation and data collection
  • Training staff and caregivers on behavior-analytic programs or content
  • Conducting assessments related to the need for behavioral intervention
  • Meeting with clients about behavior-analytic programming and services
  • Conducting behavior-analytic assessments (e.g., functional analyses, stimulus  preference assessments)• Data graphing and analysis
  • Researching the literature relevant to a current client’s programming
  • Writing and revising behavior-analytic programs

fields.text: What types of activities WILL COUNT towards your unrestricted hours requirement (formerly known as indirect hours) in pursuit of your BCBA supervised experience hours?
fields.hint:
As of 2018, the following activities are described by the board (from the BACB's website, accessed May 2019):

 

Acceptable Activities

  • Observation and data collection
  • Training staff and caregivers on behavior-analytic programs or content
  • Conducting assessments related to the need for behavioral intervention
  • Meeting with clients about behavior-analytic programming and services
  • Conducting behavior-analytic assessments (e.g., functional analyses, stimulus  preference assessments)• Data graphing and analysis
  • Researching the literature relevant to a current client’s programming
  • Writing and revising behavior-analytic programs

 

Unacceptable Activities

Only behavior-analytic activities may be counted toward experience requirements. Non-behavior-analytic activities, while valuable, may not be counted. Examples of activities that will not count as experience include (but are not limited to):

  • Attending meetings with little or no behavior-analytic content
  • Providing interventions that are not based in behavior analysis
  • Performing nonbehavioral administrative activities
  • Non-behavior-analytic trainings related to service delivery (e.g., crisis management, CPR, billing systems)
  • Completing nonbehavioral assessments (e.g., diagnostic assessments, intellectual assessments), paperwork, documentation, billing, or any other activities that are not directly related to behavior analysis
  • Attending professional conferences, workshops, or university courses
  • Didactic-course assignments

fields.text: Which of the following experimental designs does this graph most closely resemble?
fields.hint:
The above graph exemplifies an A-B design, one of the most simplistic types of designs. You do a baseline phase (no intervention), and then you intervene. Simple as that.

In the applied setting, where outcomes are king, this type of design is fine. In an experimental setting, you would be concerned that this graph does not do much to assuage any fears that the alleged functional relationship displayed here could be confounded by some extraneous variable.

For example, imagine that the person who's behavior is being measured in the graph happened to be experiencing a sore throat and a really bad headache during sessions 1 - 9 due to a new medication the behavior analyst was unaware of. Without further manipulations of the independent variable (i.e., withdrawal and re-presentation of treatment), it is hard to rule out those types of confounding variables, or "unknown unknowns."

fields.text:
The following elements are present in a skill acquisition plan that Sam, an RBT, is using:

1. The materials, antecedents, etc.

2. The consequences for correct/incorrect responding

3. How often to run the program + what contexts

 

What components, if any, are missing?
fields.hint:
The following are examples of essential components of a skill acquisition program:

1. Materials - the things you may need to use for this program (can be combined w/ #2, below).

2. Antecedents - your prompts and your SD (discriminative stimuli) and motivating operations (MOs).

3. Response - the definition of the target behavior

4. Consequences - reinforcement, punishment, etc. for various behavior

5. Error-Correction - what to do if the target behavior does not occur.

fields.text:
Samantha is working with a young client who is learning to ask for snacks after school. Immediately, when she observes her client reaching for the snack drawer, she reaches for the client's hands, and the client allows her to position them into the manual sign (ASL) for "eat." She then immediately gives her a few pieces of crackers.

After doing this for some time, Samantha notices her client is now putting her arms out in a motion that makes it easier for her to prompt her. Noticing this, Samantha then begins to provide prompting only at the wrist, waiting 5 - 10 seconds before molding her fingers into the sign for "eat." After a few trials, her client begins to independently bring her fingers into the position all by herself!

Encouraged by this, Samantha begins to provide very minor physical assistance at the client's elbow, and the child begins to closely approximate the correct sign without much support at all. 

 

What type of procedure is being used by Samantha to teach her client to ask for snacks?
fields.hint: Samantha is teaching her client

fields.text: Which of the following is the most OBSERVABLE definition of a behavior?
fields.hint:
An observable behavior definition is a behavior that is defined by outwardly visible characteristics.

 

Examples of observable behavior:

•  smiling

•  tapping your foot

•  covering your eyes

 

Examples of non-observable behavior:

•  feeling frustrating

•  solving a math problem in his head

•  a tickle in the back of your throat
